docs.title: Documentation and Example Files
docs.text:
This is a Stellar X documentation release, not a change to the software installed on your controller.

  • Updated jackal.gw, jackal.sddm, wheels.gw and base.sddm to use current sodero.actuator_gateway.* IDs. Download both files of each pair again; older copies can be rejected or fail to connect on current Station builds.
  • Aligned gateway, camera, IMU and Navigator node IDs in the tutorials, connection diagrams and CLI examples. Older screenshots may still display rc.* IDs.
  • Checked gateway imports, robot document loading and the unchanged warehouse map bundle against the document loaders used by the 2026-10-26 Station build. Robot geometry, actuator order, EtherCAT settings and safety limits are unchanged. Hardware motion and simulation runs were not part of this compatibility check. See Compatibility and Downloads.

docs.title: New
docs.text:
• Stellar Station. Build the robot system as a graph of nodes in the browser: gateways, controllers, sensors, navigation and your own modules. Load design documents into nodes, start and stop nodes, follow their logs, and back up the whole Station in one file. See Stellar Station.
  • Gateways. Actuator gateways for EtherCAT drives and robots in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, created in the new Gateway Designer (.gw). Camera and IMU gateways for simulated and real sensors; the Device Bridge serves real RGB-D cameras and IMUs. See Gateways.
  • Strider. Controller and web UI for wheeled mobile bases: differential, skid steer, mecanum, swerve and Ackermann drives (.sddm). See Strider.
  • Articulation. Joint-level controller for legged robots, humanoids and other articulated robots (.sdda). See Articulation.
  • Localization and navigation. Camera-based localization on a map and autonomous navigation to goals, configured by one map bundle (.nav). See Localization and Navigation.
  • Isaac Bridge. Extension for Isaac Sim 6.0 that connects Isaac Sim to the Station's gateways: several robots per scene, cameras and IMUs. See Simulation.
  • SSH Workspace. A Linux workspace on the controller with the sodero command-line tool and support for AI coding agents. See SSH Workspace.
  • Network Settings. A settings page on port 3000 for the LAN address and SSH access. See Network Settings.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Stellar Designer opens from a controller node on the Station and edits that node's document: manipulators (.sdd), mobile robots (.sddm) and articulated robots (.sdda). Motor and EtherCAT settings moved to the Gateway Designer.
  • Stellar Motion Studio has a new interface with the Home, Tool and Pose pages. Programs run from the SSH Workspace or as modules on the Station.

docs.title: Documentation Revisions
docs.text:
The software version stays 2.0.0; these are revisions of this documentation and its example files (Compatibility and Downloads).

  • 2026.10.21. New pages: Learning Path, Test Console, Stop Controls and Compatibility and Downloads. The map bundle page is split into Load and Configure a Map, Create a Map from Your Site and Map Bundle Format; writing Device Bridge drivers and building modules moved to Extend & Automate. The LAN ports and the test console conditions are described the same way on every page. Example files: jackal.sddm and base.sddm no longer carry run-time settings that the controller does not use. Copies downloaded before this date keep working.

docs.title: Release
docs.text: • Stellar Designer for manipulators, Stellar Motion Studio, and NVIDIA Isaac Sim integration. The v1 documentation remains available in the version selector.

docs.title: Articulation
docs.text:
The Articulation controller drives an articulated robot joint by joint: legged robots, humanoids, grippers, pan-tilt heads, or any set of joints that receives joint targets. Unlike Motion Studio, it uses no arm kinematics (no DH parameters, no Cartesian motions). It bounds and forwards joint targets from an upper controller, such as the Legged locomotion node that runs a walking policy, and it lets you jog and calibrate the joints by hand.

Item Value Node sodero.amc.NAME Document .sdda (Stellar Designer) Joints 1 to 64, driven by one actuator gateway Units rad, rad/s, N·m 
flowchart TB
    IMU["IMU gateway"] -- imu --> LL["Legged locomotion<br>walking policy"]
    LL -- "joint targets" --> AC["Articulation"]
    AC -- servo_link --> GW["Actuator gateway"]

docs.title: 1. The Document
docs.text:
An .sdda document lists the joints and how the gateway's actuators drive them.

Per joint Meaning Name Joint name Position min / max Range of motion; targets outside it are refused Velocity max Velocity limit; also the reference for the jog speed Torque max Torque limit; the controller clamps its total output to it Offset (optional) Joint position at actuator position zero Kp, Kd (optional) Stiffness and damping, for PD torque control

Drive mode. In position mode the controller bounds the joint targets and the drive (or the simulated joint) follows them with its own position control. In pd_torque mode the controller computes a PD torque from Kp and Kd and sends torque commands.

Actuator mapping. As for manipulators, influence factors connect actuators to joints; one actuator can move several joints and several actuators can move one joint, as long as the mapping is invertible.

Watchdogs. The controller switches the servo off and latches a stop when the gateway's feedback is older than 100 ms or when no new target arrives for 200 ms (the defaults). Click Clear stop, then Servo on. Reconnecting never switches the servo on by itself.

docs.title: 2. Open the Articulation UI
docs.text:
Start the gateway and the Articulation node, then click Articulation in the node's CONTROL section.

Area Contents Left rail Joints (joint monitor), Constraints (configured limits), Set origin Top bar Servo on, Servo off, Stop (switches the servo off and latches a stop), Clear stop (releases it while the servo is off), the control mode, and the button that opens the Joint control panel Status strip Servo On/Off, Feedback age in milliseconds, Safety (Ready or the reason for a stop) Controller The Articulation node this window controls Joint monitor Per joint: position, velocity, effort and target

Stop the upper controller first. Pause or stop Legged locomotion (or any program that sends joint targets) before you jog or calibrate by hand.

docs.title: 3. Jog Joints
docs.text:
1. Open the Joint control panel (button at the right of the top bar).
  2. Click Servo on.
  3. Under Joint jog, set the Speed (1–100 % of each joint's velocity limit; 10 % by default).
  4. Hold − or + next to a joint. The joint moves while you hold the button and holds its position when you release it. A jog button also switches the servo on if it is off.

Leaving the window, switching to another tab or losing the connection switches the servo off.

docs.title: 4. Send Joint Targets
docs.text:
Under Joint targets:

  1. Click Use measured positions to copy the current positions into the target fields.
  2. Change the targets of the joints you want to move.
  3. Click Stream targets. The controller follows the targets while the stream runs; Stop target stream ends it and switches the servo off.

docs.title: 5. Set the Origin
docs.text:
Set origin assigns an angle to the current position of a joint, for example after an encoder was replaced:

  1. Bring the joint to a known position.
  2. Choose the joint, then click Reset current angle to 0, or enter the true angle (deg or rad) and click Set current angle.

The servo switches off first; the joint does not move. Afterwards the servo stays off and a stop is latched: check the joint monitor, click Clear stop, then Servo on.

Some devices only support setting the origin to zero, and robots in simulation do not support it.

docs.title: 6. Control from Programs
docs.text: From How A walking robot The Legged locomotion node runs a walking policy and sends joint targets to this node The SSH workspace sodero tools call articulation.get_status, articulation.get_joint_state, articulation.servo_on, articulation.uc_pos, articulation.stop (sodero CLI); sodero articulations get shows the joints and actuators A module on the Station A module node connected to the Articulation node (Create Custom Modules)

docs.title: Motion Studio
docs.text: Stellar Motion Studio is the controller UI for manipulators. A Motion Studio node (sodero.mmc.NAME) runs the arm's real-time controller: kinematics, dynamics, trajectory generation and safety limits from the arm's .sdd document. The Motion Studio web UI lets you watch the arm in 3D, jog it, define tools and teach poses.

docs.title: 1. Open Motion Studio
docs.text:
1. On the Station, add a Motion Studio node and an Actuator gateway, load the .sdd and .gw documents and connect servo_link (Nodes and Connections).
  2. Start the gateway, then the Motion Studio node.
  3. Click Stellar Motion Studio in the node's CONTROL section. Motion Studio opens in a new tab for that arm.

docs.title: 2. Screen Layout
docs.text: The Home page No. Item Description 1 Pages Home, Tool and Pose 2 3D view The arm in its current pose, with its 3D model from the .sdd 3 Joint Status Per joint: position, target position, velocity, target velocity, effort and residual effort 4 TCP Status Position and orientation of the tool center point, and its linear and angular velocity 5 Active Tool Status The active tool's TCP offset, center of mass and payload mass 6 Filters Shows or hides the cards of the Home page

docs.title: Header
docs.text:
The header No. Item Description 1 Robot and role The controller node and whether this window has control (Pilot - Control Active) 2 Manual / Auto Manual limits the linear speed of the tool center point in the controller's own motions and jogs, 0.25 m/s by default. It is a software limit for teaching, not a safety-rated reduced speed, and it does not limit rotations or Hand mode. Auto runs at the programmed speed. 3 Feed rate Speed override in percent (10–150 %), applied to motion in progress 4 Error Reset Clears a protective stop (a joint at its limit, a speed or torque limit, a detected collision) and resets drive faults. Switch the servo on again afterwards. If the arm stays stopped, stop and start the Motion Studio node. 5 Units mm / g / deg or m / kg / radian 6 Jog Opens the jog panel 7 Command log Commands sent from this window 8 Alarm Active alarms and notifications

The Stellar mark at the top left opens the menu: Back to Stellar Station, File (import and export tools and poses), Set origin, Help & Feedback and About Stellar Motion Studio.

The menu

docs.title: 3. Jog the Arm
docs.text:
Click Jog in the header to open the jog panel.

The jog panel
  1. Switch Servo On ⑥.
  2. In JOG OPTION ②, choose the jog Mode ③:
    • Joint: move one joint at a time (J1…Jn).
    • Base: move the tool in the robot's base frame (X, Y, Z, RX, RY, RZ).
    • Tool: move the tool in its own frame.
    • Hand: hand guiding. The arm compensates gravity so you can move it by hand; the jog buttons are disabled. There is no damping and no speed limit, and collision detection stays active, so a firm push can cause a protective stop.
  3. Choose Continuous (moves while you hold a button) or Step (5° or 10 mm per click) ④, and the Speed ⑤ (50 %, 100 % or 150 %, about 0.04, 0.1 and 0.2 m/s at the tool).
  4. Hold − or + next to a joint or axis in JOG CONTROL ⑦. Motion stops when you release the button.

The POSE section ① shows the current TCP pose and joint positions.

Keep the hardware emergency stop within reach. Motion Studio has no on-screen emergency stop (Stop Controls). A continuous jog moves until the page receives the release of the button: if the browser or the connection fails while you hold it, the motion continues. Do not leave the window while jogging, and make sure the payload is set correctly before you use Hand mode.

docs.title: 4. Tools
docs.text:
The Tool page defines the tools mounted on the flange.

The Tool page
  1. Click + ① to add a tool and rename it with the pencil icon (for example gripper).
  2. Enter the TOOL CENTER POINT ③: the TCP position and orientation relative to the flange. The calculator icon ④ opens TCP Calibration, which computes the TCP from 3–10 poses that touch the same point.
  3. Enter the PAYLOAD PROPERTIES ⑤: center of mass, inertia and mass. The calculator icon ⑥ opens Payload Calibration.
  4. Click Save ⑦, or Save and Apply ⑧ to make it the active tool at once. Set as active tool ② activates a saved tool.

A wrong payload makes hand guiding and collision detection unreliable. Set the mass and center of mass of every tool you mount.

docs.title: 5. Poses
docs.text:
The Pose page stores named poses.

The Pose page
  1. Jog the arm to the pose, then click the camera icon ① (Save Current Pose). Or click + ② (Add pose) and fill in the values.
  2. Select the pose in the list ③. POSE DATA shows its TCP pose and joint positions; the icon ④ (Set from current) copies the current pose into it.
  3. TEST MOVE ⑤ moves the arm to the pose: choose Joint or Linear motion and hold Hold to move ⑥. The arm moves only while you hold the button.
  4. Click Save ⑦.

Saved poses appear as markers in the 3D view. Right-click a pose to copy it, duplicate it or delete it. Use File in the menu to export or import tools and poses.

docs.title: 6. Set the Origin
docs.text: When an absolute encoder is replaced or the arm is reassembled, set the joint origins: menu › Set origin, choose the joint, enter its true angle and click Calibration. The servo stays off afterwards.

docs.title: 7. Program the Arm
docs.text:
Motion Studio is for setup and teaching. Programs run outside the UI and call the same controller:

From How The SSH workspace sodero tools call motion.move_j, motion.move_l, motion.get_tcp_pose and the other motion.* tools (sodero CLI) A module on the Station A module node connected to the Motion Studio node's manipulator port (Create Custom Modules) 
sodero tools call motion.get_tcp_pose --input '{"target": "sodero.mmc.arm"}'
sodero tools call motion.move_j --input '{"target": "sodero.mmc.arm",
  "waypoints": [{"q": {"values": [0, 0, 1.5708, 0, 1.5708, 0]}, "vel": 0.5, "acc": 1.0}]}' --execute

Tools use SI units: radians, meters and seconds. Check a tool's arguments with sodero tools describe motion.move_j before you call it.

docs.title: Strider
docs.text:
Stellar Strider controls wheeled mobile bases. A Strider node (sodero.mlc.NAME) turns body velocities into wheel commands for its gateway, integrates odometry, and enforces the speed and acceleration limits of its .sddm document. The Strider web UI lets you jog the base, watch its state and odometry, and send navigation goals.

Supported drive types (templates of the .sddm document): differential drive, skid steer 4WD, mecanum 4WD, swerve 4WD and Ackermann.

docs.title: 1. Open Strider
docs.text:
On the Station, start the gateway first, then the Strider node (Running Nodes). Click Strider in the node's CONTROL section, or the Strider link on the node card. Strider opens in a new tab for that robot.

A running Strider node

Each Strider tab controls one robot. With several mobile robots, open one tab per robot from its own node. The Strider link on a Navigator node opens Strider directly on its Navigation page.

docs.title: 2. Screen Layout
docs.text:
The left rail has three pages: Status, Drive and Navigation. The top bar shows the readiness pill, System Log, Motion Alarm, E-STOP and the units on every page, plus the actions of the current page: Jog on Status, Stop Motion on Drive, Set Goal and Start Navigation on Navigation.

Item Description Readiness pill The current state in one line, for example Manual Drive Ready or Servo Off. Click it for the CHECKS list: Connection, Mobile base, Servo, Localization, Navigation. System Log Events of this browser session, with filters for System, Drive, Navigation and Localization Motion Alarm Active alarms and recent errors Stop Motion (Drive page) Stops manual driving and cancels a running goal E-STOP Software stop of the base: cancels driving and the navigation goal and sets the wheel speeds to zero at once, with the servo still on. It latches until Clear E-Stop, which switches the base to Idle. It does not replace the hardware emergency stop (Stop Controls). Units m / m/s / deg or m / m/s / rad. Display only; commands are always SI. The readiness checks

docs.title: 3. Status Page
docs.text:
The Status page Card Contents Trajectory (Odometry View) The path driven since the last mode change, in the odometry frame. Buttons recenter, zoom, go full screen and clear the trail. Operation Status System Ready, Moving / Motion Idle, Servo On / Off, Fault Clear / Emergency Stop / Fault / Watchdog Tripped Base Status (Odometry) Mode and X, Y, Theta, VX, VY, WZ Control Node Health Whether the base, the localizer and the navigator are reachable Drive Unit Status The drive template (for example skid_steer_4) and, per wheel, the servo state, position, velocity and target velocity Recent Events The six latest events; View All opens the System Log

Watchdog Tripped while the base stands still in Twist mode is normal: it means that no velocity command is arriving, so the base holds zero speed.

docs.title: 4. Jog the Base (Drive Page)
docs.text: The Drive page

docs.title: Step by Step
docs.text:
1. Make sure the area around the robot is clear and you can reach the emergency stop.
  2. Under Drive Mode, click Twist ①.
  3. Under Servo / Safety, switch Servo On ②. The readiness pill shows Manual Drive Ready.
  4. Set the speed limits ④: Linear Velocity Limit (default 0.2 m/s, at most 0.8 m/s) and Angular Velocity Limit.
  5. Press and hold a pad button ⑤: Forward (W), Backward (S), Turn Left (A), Turn Right (D). The base moves only while you hold the button and stops when you release it; Stop (Space) stops it too. The base slows down at the acceleration limits of its document.
  6. To drive with the keyboard, switch on Live ③ in Manual Drive, then use W, S, A, D and Space.
  7. When you are done, switch the servo off and click Idle.
No. Control Meaning 1 Drive Mode Idle: no motion; the wheels stop at once. Twist: body velocity commands (jogging and navigation). Wheel: direct wheel speeds (advanced). EMG: stops the base like E-STOP, but does not latch. 2 Servo On / Off Enables or disables the drives. Fault Reset clears drive faults; afterwards switch the servo off and on again. Clear E-Stop releases a latched E-STOP. 3 Live Sends commands at 20 Hz from the keyboard. Commands stop when the window loses focus. 4 Velocity limits Upper limits for manual driving 5 Drive pad Hold-to-drive buttons 6 Stop Motion Stops manual driving and any navigation goal 7 E-STOP Software stop that latches (Stop Controls) 8 Readiness pill Why driving is or is not possible right now

Manual commands take priority over navigation: jogging during a navigation goal overrides the navigator and can end the goal. Every manual command expires after about a second, so manual driving stops by itself if the connection drops. A navigation goal does not: cancel it with Stop Motion, Cancel or E-STOP.

docs.title: Advanced Controls
docs.text:
Click Show next to Advanced Controls for:

Section Use Wheel Direct Command each wheel's speed (Wheel mode) Preview Command See which wheel speeds a body velocity would produce, without moving (safe with the servo off) Steering Origin Set the zero angle of steered wheels Calibration Differential drive: reset odometry and calibrate wheel radius and track width by driving 1 m straight and turning half a circle Record / Replay Record a manual drive for a number of seconds and replay it

docs.title: 5. Navigation Page
docs.text:
The Navigation page appears when a Localizer and a Navigator run on the Station (Localization and Navigation).

The Navigation page after a goal was reached Card Contents Navigation Map (Occupancy Grid) The map of the loaded map bundle, the robot, the planned path and the goal. Layers: Trajectory, Global Path, Local Path, Obstacles, Robot Footprint. Drag to pan, scroll to zoom. Mission Status Running, Idle or Paused Current Pose (Map) / Goal Pose Where the robot is on the map and where it is going Localization Status Healthy, Degraded, Initializing, Relocalizing, Lost or Uninitialized, with position quality and ICP error. Global localization searches the whole map when the robot is lost. Route Summary Distance remaining, estimated time of arrival Navigator Navigator state, the base connection and a Speed Limit slider (10–100 %) Navigation Controls Set Initial Pose, Set Goal, Clear Goal, Pause, Resume, Cancel Recent Goals / Navigation Events Goals sent from this browser and their results; navigation events

docs.title: Set the Initial Pose
docs.text:
If the localization status is not Healthy, tell the localizer where the robot is:

  1. Click Set Initial Pose ①.
  2. Press on the map where the robot stands and drag in the direction it faces ②.
  3. Click Set initial pose (or Relocalize here ③ when a pose was set before).
Setting the initial pose on the map

docs.title: Send a Goal
docs.text:
1. Make sure the base is in Twist with the servo on (the readiness pill shows Navigation Ready).
  2. Click Set Goal, press on the map where the robot should go and drag in the direction it should face.
  3. Click Start Navigation. The planned path appears, and Navigator shows following.
Following the path to a goal

Pause cancels the goal and keeps it; Resume sends it again. Cancel stops navigation.

docs.title: 6. Control Strider from Programs
docs.text:
The main functions are also available to programs:

  • From the SSH workspace with sodero tools call strider.set_mode, strider.servo_on, strider.set_twist, strider.stop and strider.get_state (sodero CLI).
  • From your own modules on the Station through the mobile_base interface (Create Custom Modules).
sodero tools call strider.get_state --input '{"target": "sodero.mlc.jackal"}'
sodero tools call strider.set_mode --input '{"mode": "TWIST", "target": "sodero.mlc.jackal"}' --execute

strider.set_twist is a single velocity sample that expires after a short time. A program that drives continuously must send samples several times per second, and must stop the robot with strider.stop when it ends.

docs.title: Create Custom Modules
docs.text: A module is your own program packaged to run on the Station as a node, next to the built-in gateways and controllers. This page describes the package and how to build and install one from the SSH workspace. To install a finished package from your PC and manage installed modules, see Modules.

docs.title: 1. Package Format
docs.text:
A module package is a gzip-compressed tar archive with a package.yaml at its root:

my-module-1.0.0.tar.gz
├── package.yaml      # name, version, entry point, parameters
├── subsystem.yaml    # the node: its role and the ports it requires and provides
├── run.py            # your program (any executable)
└── ...               # your other files
File Purpose package.yaml The module's name (for example customer.patrol), version, the command that starts it and its parameters subsystem.yaml The node the module creates: its role (gateway, component, compound or app) and its ports with their contracts run.py Your program. It implements the node's lifecycle (initialize, start, stop) with the Station SDK and serves or calls the interfaces of its ports

Limits: 64 MiB per package (128 MiB unpacked).

Complete guide and examples. The SSH workspace of Stellar X contains the full package guide and runnable examples, including a status module, a navigation-goal client and a custom input gateway. Run sodero-help packages and see /opt/sodero/docs/examples/ (SSH Workspace).

docs.title: 2. Build and Install from the SSH Workspace
docs.text:
The Station SDK is not installed in the SSH workspace. Import it only in the code that runs on the Station, and give your program an offline --self-test to check it in the workspace, as the example does.

mkdir -p /workspace/my-work
cp -R /opt/sodero/docs/examples/native-status /workspace/my-work/
cd /workspace/my-work/native-status
python3 run.py --self-test                     # offline check
chmod +x run.py
tar -czf ../status-module.tar.gz package.yaml subsystem.yaml run.py README.md
sodero packages upload ../status-module.tar.gz --execute

Then add its node on the Station page (Modules › Add and Start the Module's Node), or with sodero topology add-node --kind package --package NAME --if-version N --execute, and start it. NAME is the name in package.yaml; N is the graph version that sodero topology get returns (sodero CLI).

Tip: An AI coding agent can write, check, package and install a module for you through the SSH workspace. See AI Coding Agents.

docs.title: Write Device Bridge Drivers
docs.text:
The Device Bridge runs on a small computer next to the sensors and serves their data to Stellar X. It connects any RGB-D camera, IMU or wheel board for which it has a driver: one Python class on the sensor computer. The drivers that come with the bridge, for Intel RealSense D400 cameras, the TurtleBot3 OpenCR board and simulated devices, are examples; write a driver of the same kind for your own device. Nothing on the controller is rebuilt or modified.

This page is for developers. To install the bridge and connect it to the Station, see Device Bridge.

docs.title: 1. Driver Classes
docs.text:
A driver is one Python class for one piece of hardware. It subclasses Device and each capability the hardware has: Camera, Imu or Wheels. One class may provide several, as the OpenCR driver provides both Imu and Wheels. The interfaces are documented in device_bridge/devices/base.py, and device_bridge/devices/simulated.py is the smallest complete example.

Class You implement Device open(): connect, or raise an exception with a clear message. close(): stop and release the hardware; safe to call twice. self.options holds the device's configuration block. Camera camera_info() returns CameraInfo(width, height, fx, fy, cx, cy) of the aligned output; read_frame(timeout_s) returns RgbdFrame(rgb, depth_mm, capture_unix_ns) or None Imu read_imu() returns ImuSample(gyro, accel, orientation_xyzw, source_time_ns), or None when nothing is new Wheels joint_count; read_joints() returns JointState(positions, velocities, efforts, source_time_ns) or None; set_velocities(rad_per_s); stop() sets zero speed and releases the motors

A minimal IMU driver:

# device_bridge/devices/my_imu.py
from device_bridge.devices.base import Device, Imu, ImuSample
import vendor_sdk  # placeholder: your IMU's SDK


class MyImu(Device, Imu):
    def open(self):
        self.sensor = vendor_sdk.open(self.options.get("port", "/dev/ttyUSB0"))
        self.last_ns = 0

    def close(self):
        if getattr(self, "sensor", None) is not None:
            self.sensor.close()
            self.sensor = None

    def read_imu(self):
        raw = self.sensor.latest()               # newest sample; never wait for one
        if raw is None or raw.timestamp_ns <= self.last_ns:
            return None                          # nothing new since the last call
        self.last_ns = raw.timestamp_ns
        return ImuSample(gyro=raw.gyro_rad_s,              # rad/s, sensor axes
                         accel=raw.accel_m_s2,             # m/s², gravity included
                         orientation_xyzw=raw.quaternion_xyzw,
                         source_time_ns=raw.timestamp_ns)  # must increase

Select it in the configuration as driver: device_bridge.devices.my_imu:MyImu, or register a short name in DRIVERS in device_bridge/devices/__init__.py. Keep your drivers in device_bridge/devices/ so that install.sh copies them, and add your SDK's Python package to requirements.txt. python -m unittest discover -s tests checks the bridge end to end with the simulated devices.

Rules every driver follows:

  • Units: radians, rad/s, m/s² with gravity included (+9.81 m/s² upward at rest), depth in millimeters as 16-bit integers (0 = no measurement), times in nanoseconds. Wheel positions are continuous and do not wrap at 2π.
  • Frames: IMU data in the sensor's own axes, with orientation_xyzw the sensor's attitude in the world. Camera images in the optical frame (x right, y down, z forward), depth aligned to the RGB image, both rectified without distortion. Do not rotate data into the robot's frame; the mounting belongs in the map bundle.
  • Time: source_time_ns must increase; a monotonic clock is fine. A camera's capture_unix_ns is the capture time on the wall clock.
  • Timing: read_imu and read_joints return at once; read_frame blocks for at most its timeout. Copy images out of buffers that the SDK reuses.
  • Safety: stop() must stop and release the motors. The bridge calls it when the controller switches its drive off and when commands pause for command_timeout_s.

docs.title: 2. Protocol
docs.text:
The Device Bridge and Isaac Bridge send the same messages over ZeroMQ on TCP. The bridge listens; the Station's gateways connect.

Port Direction Contents Station node 53335 bridge → controller RGB-D frames (16-bit depth in millimeters and 8-bit RGB) and the camera intrinsics Camera gateway 53334 bridge → controller IMU samples and wheel states IMU gateway, Actuator gateway 53333 controller → bridge Wheel commands: velocity while the drive is on, limp when it is off Actuator gateway

Every message carries the robot name, and each gateway takes only the messages of its own name. A slow link drops old frames instead of queuing them. The byte layouts are documented in docs/protocol.md in the repository.

docs.title: Device Bridge
docs.text:
Stellar X connects to the rest of the robot through network ports only. Sensors that need USB, such as an Intel RealSense depth camera or a USB IMU, therefore go on a small computer next to them: a Raspberry Pi, another single-board computer or a PC. The Device Bridge runs on that computer. It reads the devices and serves their data to the controller over the LAN.

The bridge speaks the same network protocol as Isaac Bridge, so the controller's built-in Camera gateway, IMU gateway, Visual odometry, Localizer and Navigator connect to real sensors the same way as to a simulated robot: they connect to the sensor computer instead of the Isaac Sim computer. Real sensors still need their own values: camera intrinsics, mounting and synchronized clocks.

Use the Device Bridge when:

  • the robot carries a USB camera or IMU, which cannot plug into the controller;
  • the motor board of a small robot sits on USB as well (for example the TurtleBot3 OpenCR board) and the controller should drive it.

Drives on the controller's EtherCAT port do not need the bridge, and neither does a simulated robot.

You want to Page Install the bridge, configure its devices and connect it to the Station This page Add a driver for your own camera, IMU or wheel board Write Device Bridge Drivers

The Device Bridge is an open-source program that works with any RGB-D camera, IMU or wheel board through drivers. It comes with example drivers for Intel RealSense D400 cameras, the TurtleBot3 OpenCR board and simulated devices (Built-in Drivers); other devices connect through a driver that you add. Nothing changes on the controller when you install the bridge or add a driver.

docs.title: 1. Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph SC ["Sensor computer"]
        DB(["Device Bridge"])
        RS["RealSense<br>depth camera"] --> DB
        IU["USB IMU"] --> DB
        MB["Motor board<br>(optional)"] <--> DB
    end
    subgraph SX ["Stellar X · Stellar Station"]
        CG["Camera gateway"]
        IG["IMU gateway"]
        AG["Actuator gateway<br>(optional)"]
        VO["Visual odometry"]
        LO["Localizer"]
        NV["Navigator"]
        ST["Strider"]
    end
    DB -->|"53335 · RGB-D frames"| CG
    DB -->|"53334 · IMU samples"| IG
    DB <-->|"53333 commands · 53334 joint states"| AG
    CG --> VO
    IG --> VO
    CG --> LO
    VO -->|odometry| LO
    LO -->|"localization · map"| NV
    NV -->|mobile_base| ST
    AG <-->|servo_link| ST

The bridge listens on three ports and the controller's gateways connect to it, exactly as they connect to the simulator. Every message carries the bridge's robot_name, and each gateway takes the data published under the name it is configured with. Without the optional wheel stream, Strider drives the robot's own base through an EtherCAT Actuator gateway as usual.

docs.title: 2. Requirements
docs.text:
Item Requirement Sensor computer A Raspberry Pi, another single-board computer or a PC next to the sensors, running 64-bit Linux with systemd (for example Debian 12, Raspberry Pi OS or Ubuntu). A RealSense camera needs a USB 3 port. Python Python 3.8 or later. The installer creates its own environment; when the system Python cannot load the RealSense SDK (for example Debian 12 on 64-bit ARM), it installs a standalone Python 3.10 by itself. Internet During installation only, to download the Python packages Network The sensor computer and Stellar X on the same LAN; a wired link is recommended Clocks Synchronized to within about 20 ms while frames carry their capture time (the default) Firewall Inbound TCP ports 53333–53335 on the sensor computer open to the controller IMU address Only for an IMU stream: the controller's IMU gateway connects to a sensor address that Sodero support sets for the unit. Ask Sodero support to set it to the sensor computer before you connect the IMU (IMU).

Bandwidth. RGB-D frames travel uncompressed: about 61 Mbit/s at 424 × 240 and 15 fps, about 185 Mbit/s at 640 × 480 and 15 fps, and about 370 Mbit/s at 640 × 480 and 30 fps. IMU samples and wheel messages add only a few Mbit/s. Use a wired link, ideally Gigabit Ethernet, for the higher settings.

Clock synchronization. With send_capture_time: true (the default), every frame carries its capture time. The controller accepts a frame only when that time is at most 20 ms ahead of its own clock and at most 2 s old, so run NTP (for example chrony) to keep both computers on the same time. If you cannot synchronize the clocks, set send_capture_time: false: the controller then uses each frame's arrival time, as with the simulator. This needs no clock agreement and costs the network delay in accuracy.

Tip: On a sensor computer that runs ufw, open the ports for the controller with sudo ufw allow from ROBOT_ADDRESS to any port 53333:53335 proto tcp.

docs.title: 3. Install and Run
docs.text:
1. Get the source on the sensor computer:

    git clone https://github.com/Sodero-labs/device_bridge.git
cd device_bridge

    You can also copy the device_bridge folder to the sensor computer by other means, for example with scp -r from your PC.

  2. Choose a configuration. Copy the example closest to your hardware, for example cp config/turtlebot3_d435.yaml config/my_robot.yaml, and edit it as described in Configuration File. config/turtlebot3_d435.yaml serves a RealSense D435 and the IMU of a TurtleBot3 OpenCR board, with the wheel stream prepared but commented out; config/simulated.yaml needs no hardware.

  3. Install and start the service:

    sudo deploy/install.sh config/my_robot.yaml

    The installer copies the program and your configuration to /opt/sodero-device-bridge (as config.yaml), creates a Python environment there and installs the sodero-device-bridge service. The service starts now and at every boot, and restarts 3 seconds after an error. It runs as the user who called sudo, with access to serial ports, USB devices and cameras.

  4. Follow the log with journalctl -u sodero-device-bridge -f and look for the lines in Log Lines.

  5. Check the streams from another computer, as described in Check from Another Computer.

To change a setting later, edit /opt/sodero-device-bridge/config.yaml and run sudo systemctl restart sodero-device-bridge.

Running install.sh again, for example after git pull, replaces /opt/sodero-device-bridge/config.yaml with the file you pass. Keep your configuration in your own file and pass it every time.

docs.title: Configuration File
docs.text:
The configuration names the robot, lists the devices on this computer and states which stream each device feeds. Every stream is optional; the bridge opens only the ports of the streams you configure.

robot_name: tb3              # the controller finds this robot's data under this name

network:                     # optional; these are the defaults
  bind: 0.0.0.0              # every interface, or this computer's LAN address
  command_port: 53333        # controller -> bridge: wheel commands
  state_port: 53334          # bridge -> controller: IMU samples and wheel states
  camera_port: 53335         # bridge -> controller: RGB-D frames and intrinsics

state_poll_hz: 200           # optional; how often the IMU and wheel devices are read

devices:                     # the hardware, each under a name you choose
  d435:
    driver: realsense        # a built-in driver
    serial: auto             # every other key is an option of the driver
    width: 424
    height: 240
    fps: 15
  opencr:
    driver: turtlebot3_opencr
    port: /dev/turtlebot3_opencr
    max_linear_speed: 0.15   # m/s
    max_angular_speed: 1.0   # rad/s

streams:                     # what the controller receives
  camera:
    device: d435
    frame_id: cam0_optical   # the camera frame named in the map bundle
    send_capture_time: true  # needs synchronized clocks; false = arrival time
  imu:
    device: opencr           # one device can feed several streams
  wheels:                    # only when the controller drives these wheels
    device: opencr
    command_timeout_s: 0.5   # stop the wheels when commands pause this long
Key Default Description robot_name required Name under which the bridge publishes. The Station's gateways use the same name. network.bind 0.0.0.0 Address the bridge listens on. Enter the sensor computer's LAN address to restrict it to one interface. network.camera_port 53335 RGB-D frames. Must match the Camera gateway's Port. network.state_port 53334 IMU samples and wheel states. Keep the default: the IMU and Actuator gateways expect it. network.command_port 53333 Wheel commands. Keep the default. state_poll_hz 200 How often the IMU and wheel drivers are polled, per second devices.<name>.driver required A built-in driver or your own class as package.module:Class. All other keys of the block are passed to the driver as options. streams.camera.device — The device that provides the camera streams.camera.frame_id cam0_optical Optical frame name sent with each frame, 1 to 15 bytes streams.camera.send_capture_time true Send each frame's capture time. false: the controller uses the arrival time. streams.imu.device — The device that provides the IMU streams.wheels.device — The device that drives the wheels. Leave the stream out when the controller drives its own base. streams.wheels.command_timeout_s 0.5 Stop the wheels when commands pause this long, in seconds

Unknown keys are refused, so a typo stops the bridge with a clear message instead of being ignored. The configuration needs at least one device and one stream, and each stream must name a listed device that provides it.

Tip: Choose a robot_name of lowercase letters, digits and underscores that starts with a letter, such as tb3. Every Station node accepts such a name, so the gateway nodes can carry the same name.

docs.title: Log Lines
docs.text:
After a start with config/turtlebot3_d435.yaml (camera and IMU, no wheel stream), the log shows these lines (time stamps left out):

INFO device_bridge: device 'd435' (realsense) is open
INFO device_bridge: device 'opencr' (turtlebot3_opencr) is open
INFO device_bridge.bridge: camera 424x240 fx=303.22 fy=303.26 cx=216.20 cy=123.18 frame_id=cam0_optical (use these intrinsics in the controller's camera settings)
INFO device_bridge.bridge: serving robot 'tb3' on 0.0.0.0 (camera 53335, state 53334, command -)
INFO device_bridge: camera_pair 15.0/s, imu_state 50.0/s, sim_state 0.0/s, sim_command 0.0/s
Line Meaning device '…' (…) is open The driver has connected to its hardware. camera 424x240 fx=… fy=… cx=… cy=… The camera's resolution and intrinsics. Enter them in the Camera gateway (see Camera). serving robot 'tb3' on … (camera 53335, state 53334, command -) The robot name and the ports served. - marks a stream that is not configured. camera_pair 15.0/s, imu_state 50.0/s, … Message rates, every 10 seconds. sim_command counts the commands received from the controller.

If the configuration or a device fails, the log shows one ERROR line that names the problem, and the service tries again 3 seconds later.

docs.title: Check from Another Computer
docs.text:
listen receives the streams the way the controller does. Run it from a copy of the source on any computer on the same network, for example your PC:

cd device_bridge
python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install numpy pyzmq PyYAML
python -m device_bridge.listen SENSOR_COMPUTER_ADDRESS --robot tb3

It prints one line per message kind with its rate and latest values, for example:

camera_info     1.0/s  width=424 height=240 fx=303.217 fy=303.257 cx=216.198 cy=123.175
camera_pair    15.0/s  424x240, depth valid 91%, median 1480 mm, capture age 9 ms (meaningful with synchronized clocks)
imu_state      50.0/s  gyro [+0.002, -0.001, +0.000] rad/s, |accel| 9.80 m/s^2

To test the wheels, add --wheels with one speed per wheel in rad/s, for example --wheels 1.0 1.0 --seconds 2. listen drives them for --seconds and then releases them the way the controller does.

--wheels moves the robot. Lift the wheels off the ground or give the robot room, and stop the Station's Actuator gateway for this robot first.

docs.title: Try Without Hardware
docs.text:
config/simulated.yaml serves a test-pattern camera, a slowly turning IMU and two ideal wheels under the robot name tb3. Use it to try the network, the Station's gateway settings and listen before the hardware is ready. Install it as a service, or run it in the foreground in the environment from the previous section:

sudo deploy/install.sh config/simulated.yaml     # as a service
python -m device_bridge config/simulated.yaml    # or in the foreground; stop with Ctrl+C

docs.title: 4. Built-in Drivers
docs.text:
The bridge comes with these drivers. They are ready to use and serve as examples: other cameras, IMUs and wheel boards connect through a driver that you add (Write Device Bridge Drivers).

Driver Provides Options (default) realsense Camera serial (auto), width (424), height (240), fps (15) turtlebot3_opencr IMU and wheels (left, right) port (/dev/turtlebot3_opencr), poll_hz (100, 20 to 100), max_linear_speed (0.15 m/s, at most 0.22), max_angular_speed (1.0 rad/s, at most 2.84) simulated_camera Camera width (424), height (240), fps (15) simulated_imu IMU rate_hz (100), yaw_rate (0.1 rad/s) simulated_wheels Wheels joints (2), rate_hz (100) package.module:Class What the class provides Your own driver (Write Device Bridge Drivers)
  • realsense reads Intel RealSense D400 cameras through the RealSense SDK and is tested with the D435. Depth is aligned to the color image, so both share the color camera's intrinsics. With serial: auto, exactly one camera must be connected; with several cameras, enter the serial number.
  • turtlebot3_opencr drives the OpenCR board of a TurtleBot3 Burger running the ROBOTIS TurtleBot3 ROS 2 firmware. The board is both the wheel controller and the IMU, and its serial port can have only one owner, so one device feeds both the imu and the wheels stream. Wheel speeds are scaled down together to the configured limits, which keeps the path's curvature. If the bridge stops talking to the board, the firmware stops the wheels by itself within 0.5 s. Set port to the board's serial device (for example /dev/ttyACM0) when the default device name does not exist on your system.
  • simulated_camera, simulated_imu and simulated_wheels stand in for hardware: a moving color pattern in front of a flat wall 2 m away, a level sensor turning slowly about its z axis, and joints that follow their velocity commands exactly.

docs.title: 5. Connect It on the Station Page
docs.text:
Start with the bridge running and listen showing its streams, then open the Station page (http://ROBOT_ADDRESS). The steps use the robot name tb3; use your bridge's robot_name instead.

Names must match. The Camera gateway's Camera name, the IMU gateway's Robot in World and the Actuator gateway's Robot name must all be exactly the bridge's robot_name. Each gateway takes only the data published under its name.

docs.title: Camera
docs.text:
1. Click Add node, choose Gateway › Camera gateway and name it after the robot, for example tb3 (node sodero.camera_gateway.tb3).
  2. In the CAMERA GATEWAY section of the inspector, enter:
    • Camera name: the bridge's robot_name (tb3). The bridge publishes its camera under the robot name; it has no separate camera name.
    • Camera host: SENSOR_COMPUTER_ADDRESS.
    • Port: 53335, or the bridge's network.camera_port.

  3. Enter the resolution and intrinsics from the bridge's camera … log line. A new Camera gateway computes its intrinsics from a field of view, as for a simulated camera, so for intrinsics its CAMERA SETTINGS show horizontal fov deg but not fx, fy, cx and cy. Load the calibrated values once with Upload yaml while the node is stopped:

    camera_gateway:
  camera:
    type: isaac_zmq              # the simulator's stream format, which the bridge speaks
    frame_id: cam0_optical       # the bridge's streams.camera.frame_id
    width: 424                   # resolution from the log line
    height: 240
    fps: 15
    isaac:
      robot_name: tb3            # Camera name: the bridge's robot_name
      host: SENSOR_COMPUTER_ADDRESS
      port: 53335
    intrinsics:
      mode: manual               # use fx, fy, cx, cy instead of a field of view
      fx: 303.22
      fy: 303.26
      cx: 216.20
      cy: 123.18

    After the upload, CAMERA SETTINGS shows these values and you can change them there later. Check that Camera name, Camera host and Port show your values.

  4. Click Start.

Intrinsics belong to one resolution. After you change the bridge's width, height or camera, enter the new values from its log line.

Tip: In the SSH workspace, sodero camera snapshot sodero.camera_gateway.tb3 --output frame.png saves a picture from the gateway.

docs.title: IMU
docs.text:
1. Click Add node, choose Gateway › IMU gateway and name it after the robot (tb3).
  2. In IMU SETTINGS, check that Robot in World is the bridge's robot_name (a new IMU gateway starts with its node name) and click Save settings.
  3. Start the gateway.

The IMU gateway has no address field: it connects to the sensor address that Sodero support sets for the unit (Requirements).

docs.title: Wheels (Optional)
docs.text:
Only when the bridge serves a wheels stream:

  1. Add an Actuator gateway and load a simulation .gw (hardware.type: simulation) whose joints are the bridge's wheels, in the same order (turtlebot3_opencr: left, then right).
  2. In its TARGET section, click Change, enter Robot name tb3 and Sim host SENSOR_COMPUTER_ADDRESS, and click Done.
  3. Add Strider with your base's .sddm and connect its servo_link to the Actuator gateway's servo_link.
  4. Drive slowly at first, with the wheels off the ground.

The bridge stops and releases the wheels when the controller switches its drive off and when commands pause for longer than command_timeout_s. Keep someone ready to stop the robot during the first runs.

docs.title: Navigation and Mounting
docs.text:
1. Add Visual odometry, Localizer and Navigator and connect them as for any robot: the Camera gateway's camera to Visual odometry and the Localizer, the IMU gateway's imu to Visual odometry, Visual odometry's (or Strider's) odometry to the Localizer, the Localizer's localization and map to the Navigator, and Strider's mobile_base to the Navigator.
  2. Upload the map bundle (.nav) once to the Localizer. The Navigator uses the same shared bundle (Load and Configure a Map).

The bridge sends camera and IMU data in the sensors' own frames. Where the sensors sit on the robot, their mounting extrinsics, belongs in the map bundle (Load and Configure a Map): measure the mounting and enter it there, and do not rotate data inside a driver. Keep the bridge's frame_id, the Camera gateway's frame id and the camera frame of the map bundle the same (default cam0_optical).

docs.title: 6. Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix The service restarts every few seconds and the log shows one ERROR line A configuration or device problem named in that line, such as an unknown key, a stream without its device, RealSense … is not connected or no reply from the board Fix the configuration or the connection, then restart the service listen prints no messages from … for robot '…' The bridge is not running, --robot differs from robot_name, or a firewall blocks the ports Check systemctl status sodero-device-bridge, use the name from the serving robot line, open TCP 53333–53335 Camera gateway: Waiting for simulator at …:53335 Wrong Camera host or Port, no camera stream, or a firewall Compare with the serving robot line and run listen from another computer Camera gateway: … publishes frames of camera(s) 'tb3' but none of camera '…' Camera name differs from robot_name Set Camera name to robot_name, then Stop and Start Camera gateway: Frames … are stale or carry capture times that do not match this Station's clock (clock skew?) The clocks differ: frames look more than 20 ms in the future or more than 2 s old Synchronize the clocks with NTP, or set send_capture_time: false and restart the bridge Visual odometry drifts or the Localizer does not fit the map Field-of-view intrinsics instead of the calibrated ones, or values for another resolution Upload the intrinsics from the bridge's log line for the current resolution The IMU gateway does not start: Start the project World to provide the simulation IMU endpoint. No simulator/sensor address is configured for the unit Ask Sodero support to set it to the sensor computer The IMU gateway runs, but no IMU data arrives Robot in World differs from robot_name, the bridge has no imu stream (state -), or the unit's address points to another computer Fix the name or the stream; check the address with Sodero support The wheels do not move No wheels stream (command -), a different Robot name, commands that are not velocity commands (modes … are not velocity control), or the OpenCR motor power is off (wheel motors are not powered) Add the stream, fix the name, drive Strider in Twist mode, switch on the motor power The wheels stop while driving; log: no wheel command for 0.50 s: wheels stopped The safety watchdog: commands paused longer than command_timeout_s Use a wired link; raise command_timeout_s only with care The camera_pair rate stays below fps Not enough bandwidth (Wi-Fi), a USB 2 port or a busy sensor computer Use a wired link and a USB 3 port, or lower width, height or fps Camera host cannot be edited The camera address is set for this unit Ask Sodero support to point it at the sensor computer

docs.title: EtherCAT Gateway
docs.text:
Stellar X is an EtherCAT master. An actuator gateway of type EtherCAT drives CiA 402 servo drives on the controller's EtherCAT port with distributed-clock synchronization at the gateway's control period (1 ms by default). This page covers wiring, the gateway document, parameters, bring-up and troubleshooting.

For a complete example from wiring to driving, see EtherCAT Mobile Base: four drives on a skid-steer base, with example files.

Real motors move. Bring up a new EtherCAT system with the robot clear of people and obstacles, the drives' safe torque off (STO) and emergency stop wired, and someone at the emergency stop (Stop Controls).

docs.title: 1. What You Need
docs.text:
Item Requirement Drives EtherCAT servo drives with the CiA 402 profile, supporting cyclic synchronous position (CSP). Mobile bases also need cyclic synchronous velocity (CSV); torque control needs cyclic synchronous torque (CST). Drive data The drive's ESI file (EtherCAT Slave Information, .xml) from the manufacturer, unless the drive is in the built-in catalog Motor data Rated and peak torque, maximum speed, encoder resolution, gear ratio Cables Standard EtherCAT (Ethernet) cables, one per drive

Built-in catalog: Panasonic MINAS A6BE, RS Automation CSD7, MyActuator RMD-X (EtherCAT) drives, and Panasonic MSMD, RS Automation CSMA/CSMT and MyActuator RMD-X motors.

docs.title: 2. Wire the Drives
docs.text:
Connect the drives as a line, starting at Stellar X:

flowchart LR
    SX["Stellar X"] --> D1["Drive 1"]
    D1 --> D2["Drive 2"]
    D2 --> D3["Drive 3"]
  • Plug Stellar X's EtherCAT Out port into the IN port of the first drive. Connect each drive's OUT port to the next drive's IN port.
  • Do not use a network switch. EtherCAT frames must pass through the drives in a line.
  • The cable order is the actuator order. The first drive on the cable is actuator 1 (index 0) of the gateway, the second is actuator 2 (index 1), and so on. To change the order, change the wiring.
  • Devices after the last controlled drive are allowed; the gateway ignores them.
  • The EtherCAT port needs no IP address and is not configured on the Network Settings page.

docs.title: 3. Create the Gateway Document
docs.text:
1. On the Station, add an Actuator gateway node, for example arm (Nodes and Connections).
  2. Click Edit Stellar Gateway Designer. In Create gateway definition, choose EtherCAT and click Next › Create (Gateway Designer).
  3. Click Add Actuator once per drive, in cable order.
  4. For each actuator, fill in the Motor tab and the EtherCAT tab as described below.
  5. Open 02 Verification, click Verify and fix any errors.
An EtherCAT gateway with two actuators; the EtherCAT tab of actuator 1

docs.title: Motor Tab
docs.text:
Motor tab

Click Brand, Series or Model ① to open Motor Select: search by model number, or pick Brand › Series › Model. The preview shows the catalog values, and Accept fills them in. For a motor that is not in the catalog, type the values.

Motor Select catalog: search ①, or pick Brand ② › Series ③ › Model ④, then Accept ⑤

The fields of the Motor tab:

Section Field Unit Meaning ② TORQUE Rated torque Nm Continuous motor torque. Torque commands are sent to the drive in per mille of this value. Max torque Nm Peak torque of the motor itself, at the motor shaft (the motor's datasheet value, not the torque after the reducer). The gateway limits torque commands to Max torque × Gear ratio at the joint. ③ SPEED Max speed rpm Maximum speed of the motor itself, at the motor shaft (the motor's datasheet value, not the joint speed after the reducer). The gateway limits velocity commands to Max speed ÷ Gear ratio at the joint. ④ MOTOR CHARACTERISTICS Resolution PPR Encoder pulses (counts) per motor revolution, before the gear, e.g. 1,048,576 (2²⁰) or 8,388,608 (2²³) ⑤ ENCODER CONFIGURATION Encoder offset pulses Absolute encoder zero. Set by origin calibration in Motion Studio; leave 0 for a new robot. ⑥ REDUCER Gear ratio – Motor turns per joint turn

Rated torque, Max torque and Max speed are the motor's own values at the motor shaft, as in the motor's datasheet, whatever reducer follows it. Do not convert them to the joint side: the gateway applies the Gear ratio itself.

If Gear ratio is exactly 1, the gateway reads the gear ratio configured in the drive itself (object 0x6091). Enter the real ratio when the drive does not hold it.

docs.title: EtherCAT Tab
docs.text:
Click the gear icon in the actuator panel to open Servo Driver Select:

Search ① or pick Brand ③ › Series ④ › Model ⑤, or import the drive's ESI file ②. Accept ⑥ fills in the EtherCAT tab.
  • Pick the drive from the catalog, or click ESI Import ② and choose the drive's ESI .xml. If the file describes several devices, choose yours; then choose the RxPDO and TxPDO areas to use.
  • Accept fills in the drive's identification, start-up SDOs and PDO mapping. Values you change later are highlighted; click one to return to the catalog value.
IDENTIFICATION ①, SDOS ②, PDOS ③ Section Field Meaning IDENTIFICATION Idx Position of the drive on the cable, from 0 (read-only) Alias An alias that identifies the device (read-only). The gateway addresses drives by their position on the cable, not by alias. Name A label for logs SDOS Index, Subindex, Value, Size Start-up parameters written to the drive before operation. Index, subindex and value are hexadecimal (0x…); size is in bytes. The entry named Absolute Encoder Reset is not written at start-up; Motion Studio's origin calibration uses it. PDOS Rx PDO / Tx PDO index The PDO mapping objects, typically 0x1600 and 0x1A00 Entries The objects exchanged every cycle (see below). Init Value sets a constant for extra RxPDO entries.

docs.title: Process Data
docs.text:
The gateway uses these CiA 402 objects:

Direction Object Name Required RxPDO (to drive) 0x6040 Controlword Yes 0x607A Target position For position control 0x60FF Target velocity For velocity control (mobile bases) 0x6071 Target torque For torque control 0x60B2 Torque offset Optional (feed-forward) 0x6060 Modes of operation Optional (also written by SDO) TxPDO (from drive) 0x6041 Statusword Yes 0x6064 Position actual value Yes 0x606C Velocity actual value Recommended 0x6077 Torque actual value Recommended 0x6061 Modes of operation display Recommended 0x603F Error code Recommended (fault messages)

When a controller drives the gateway, you do not choose the mode of operation: the controller selects it per command. Position commands use CSP (8), velocity commands CSV (9), torque and impedance commands CST (10). In the test console you choose the drive mode yourself.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Open 02 Verification and click Verify. Open a check marked Error to see which actuator and which value to fix, then click Verify again.

Verification found missing motor parameters and encoder resolution

A Strider (mobile base) drives its wheels in velocity mode. If the drive's RxPDO has no Target velocity (0x60FF), the wheels do not move and the gateway reports it. Choose a PDO mapping that includes 0x60FF.

docs.title: 4. Connect a Controller
docs.text:
1. Add the controller node (Motion Studio, Strider or Articulation) and import its document. The document must name this gateway and its actuator indices (Design Documents).
  2. Connect the controller's servo_link to the gateway's servo_link.

docs.title: 5. Bring Up the System
docs.text:
1. Power the drives. Release the emergency stop and STO.

  2. Select the gateway and click Start node. Watch LOGS › Gateway events:

    EtherCAT: starting on network port 'eth0' (2 drive(s) expected).
EtherCAT: found drive 1 (MINAS-A6B).
EtherCAT: found drive 2 (MINAS-A6B).
EtherCAT ready: 2 drive(s) operational, 1.0 ms cycle.

  3. Optional: before you start a controller, click Test Stellar Gateway in the gateway's CONTROL section to open the test console and move single actuators. When the test is done, click Servo OFF in the console and Stop test in the gateway's CONTROL section. EtherCAT Mobile Base › Step 5 shows a complete test of four wheels.

  4. Start the controller node, open its UI and switch Servo On. Jog slowly first and check each joint's direction.

Tip: Bring up one drive first. When it reaches EtherCAT ready and moves correctly, add the next drive to the cable and to the document.

docs.title: 6. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The gateway explains every problem in Gateway events, followed by a hint. The most common messages:

Message Cause and fix EtherCAT: no cable link on network port … No Ethernet link. Plug the cable into Stellar X's EtherCAT Out port and into the first drive's IN port, and power the drive. EtherCAT: no drive answered on network port … The cable goes to the wrong port of the drive (OUT instead of IN), to a switch, or the drive has no power. EtherCAT: found M of the N drives this gateway controls. The chain ends after drive M. Check the cable from drive M's OUT port to the next drive's IN port, and that drive's power. …configuration describes K drive(s), but the gateway controls N. The drive list in the document does not match the actuators. Fix it in the Gateway Designer. Drive … exchanges x/y bits of process data …, the project describes … The PDO mapping in the document does not match the drive. Re-select the drive or re-import its ESI file. Drive … did not reach SAFE-OP / OP … The drive refused the configuration or the synchronization. The AL status in the message names the reason (sync, watchdog, PDO or cycle time). Drive … gets velocity commands, but Target Velocity (0x60FF) is not in its … Add 0x60FF to the RxPDO (see Process Data). Servo ON failed: drive … did not enable (it stays in 'switch on disabled'). The drive refuses to switch on: check its STO and enable inputs, the emergency stop and its main power. Drive … fault: … (error code 0x….) A drive alarm, such as overcurrent, voltage, temperature, encoder or following error. Read the alarm on the drive and look it up in its manual, then Error Reset / Fault Reset in the controller UI and switch the servo on again. EtherCAT communication lost: the drives stopped answering. A cable was unplugged or a drive lost power. The message names the segment; fix it and restart the gateway. No commands from the robot controller for 3.0 s: servo turned OFF for safety. The controller stopped or lost its connection. Until the 3 s pass, the gateway keeps the last command. Start the controller and switch the servo on again.

Problems that are not in the gateway's log (such as a joint moving in the wrong direction or the wrong distance) come from the documents: check the actuator order (cable order), Gear ratio, Resolution, and the joint mapping in the controller's document.

docs.title: Gateway Designer
docs.text: Stellar Gateway Designer creates and edits gateway documents (.gw): the hardware type, the list of actuators, each actuator's motor and drive parameters, and the fieldbus settings. It is part of Stellar Designer and opens from an actuator gateway node on the Station.

docs.title: 1. Open the Gateway Designer
docs.text:
1. Select an actuator gateway node on the Station.
  2. Click Edit Stellar Gateway Designer in the DEFINITION section.

The Gateway Designer opens in a new tab with the node's document. Edits are saved back to the node automatically. Stop the gateway before you edit; the Station refuses saves while it runs (Gateway '…' is running — stop it in the Station, then save again.) and while its test console is open (Gateway '…' has a test console open — stop the test in the Station, then save again.).

A simulation gateway with four actuators Area Contents Breadcrumb Where the document belongs: device / Station / node / file. The arrow returns to the Station. Steps 01 Gateway setup (actuators and their parameters) and 02 Verification Actuators (N) One card per actuator, in index order, with its brand, model and status (Configured / Not configured). Add Actuator adds one; × removes one. Actuator panel The parameters of the selected actuator, in tabs: Motor and a tab for the hardware type (EtherCAT or Isaac Sim) Units mm / g / deg or m / kg / radian for display

docs.title: 2. Choose the Hardware Type
docs.text:
A new gateway node starts with an empty document. When you open it, the Gateway Designer asks for the hardware type:

Create gateway definition Type Use Isaac Sim ① A robot in NVIDIA Isaac Sim (Simulation Gateway) EtherCAT ② CiA 402 servo drives on the EtherCAT port (EtherCAT Gateway)

Select the type and click Next ③, then Create.

To change the type of an existing gateway, click the Stellar mark at the top left and choose Definition › Replace definition. Pick the new type and click Next › Replace. Existing actuators keep their motor settings and receive the new type's hardware settings; the previous type's hardware settings are removed. This cannot be undone.

docs.title: 3. Add and Configure Actuators
docs.text:
1. Click Add Actuator once per motor. Actuator 1 is index 0, actuator 2 is index 1, and so on.
  2. Select an actuator card. Fill in the Motor tab: pick the motor from the catalog (Brand › Series › Model) or enter its values.
  3. Fill in the tab of the hardware type: EtherCAT (identification, SDOs, PDOs) or Isaac Sim (DOF offset).

docs.title: Motor Parameters
docs.text:
Field Unit Meaning Rated torque Nm Continuous torque of the motor. For EtherCAT drives it is the reference for torque commands in per mille. Max torque Nm Peak torque of the motor. The gateway clamps torque commands to Max torque × gear ratio at the joint. Max speed rpm Maximum motor speed. The gateway limits velocity commands to Max speed ÷ gear ratio at the joint. Resolution PPR Encoder pulses per motor revolution, before the gear (EtherCAT). For example 2²³ = 8,388,608 for a 23-bit encoder. Encoder offset pulses Zero offset of the absolute encoder. Normally set by origin calibration in Motion Studio, not by hand. Gear ratio ratio Motor turns per joint turn.

For simulation gateways only Max torque, Max speed and Gear ratio apply.

docs.title: 4. Verify and Export
docs.text:
Open 02 Verification and click Verify. The Gateway Designer checks the hardware type, the actuator list, the motor parameters (for EtherCAT also the encoder resolution) and the configuration files.

All checks passed

Errors (for example a parameter that must be positive) must be fixed; warnings are advisory. Then start the gateway from the Station.

When all checks pass, Export .gw downloads the document as a .gw file, which you can import into another gateway node (Import .gw).

docs.title: 5. Simulation Gateways
docs.text:
For Isaac Sim gateways, the actuator panel has an Isaac Sim tab with one setting:

The Isaac Sim tab of an actuator

DOF offset is the first joint of the Isaac Sim articulation that this gateway drives. Leave it at 0 when one gateway drives the whole robot. Several gateways can share one simulated robot, for example an arm gateway with offset 0 for joints 1–6 and a gripper gateway with offset 6 for the joints after them.

The robot name in the scene and the simulator address are set on the Station node, not in the document (Simulation Gateway).

docs.title: Gateways Overview
docs.text:
A gateway is the node that connects the Station to the physical world: motors, drives and sensors, real or simulated. Controllers never talk to hardware directly. They exchange commands and states with a gateway through a port, and the gateway translates them for the fieldbus or the simulator.

flowchart TB
    C["Controllers<br>Motion Studio · Strider · Articulation"] -- servo_link --> AG["Actuator gateway"]
    AG -- "EtherCAT" --> D["EtherCAT drives"]
    AG -- "simulation" --> I["Isaac Sim robot"]
    CG["Camera gateway"] --> N["Visual odometry · Localizer"]
    IG["IMU gateway"] --> L["Legged locomotion · Visual odometry"]
    I -. "camera" .-> CG
    I -. "IMU" .-> IG

Because only the gateway knows the hardware, the same controller and controller document can drive a simulated robot and the real one. To move from Isaac Sim to real motors, you give the robot an EtherCAT gateway document. Before you operate the real robot, verify its actuator mapping, calibration, limits and sensor settings: motor directions, gear ratios, encoder resolution and sensor mounting are properties of the hardware.

docs.title: Built-in Gateways
docs.text:
Module Node ID Connects Configured with Actuator gateway sodero.actuator_gateway.NAME EtherCAT drives, or the joints of a robot in Isaac Sim A .gw document (Gateway Designer) Camera gateway sodero.camera_gateway.NAME An RGB-D camera: a camera in Isaac Sim, or a real camera through the Device Bridge Camera settings in the inspector (Sensors and Cameras) IMU gateway sodero.imu_gateway.NAME An IMU (and foot contacts in Isaac Sim): in Isaac Sim, or through the Device Bridge IMU settings in the inspector (Sensors and Cameras)

For devices the built-in gateways do not cover, you can write your own gateway as a module with the role gateway (Create Custom Modules). Once installed, it appears in Add node › Gateway with the CUSTOM badge.

docs.title: Actuator Gateway Types
docs.text:
The .gw document chooses how the actuator gateway reaches its actuators:

Type hardware.type Use Page EtherCAT ethercat CiA 402 servo drives on the controller's EtherCAT port, synchronized by distributed clocks EtherCAT Gateway Isaac Sim simulation The joints of a robot in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, through the Isaac Bridge extension Simulation Gateway

docs.title: Actuators and Indices
docs.text:
A gateway drives a list of actuators, numbered from zero in the order they are defined (actuator 1 is index 0, actuator 2 is index 1, …). For EtherCAT, the order of the actuators is the order of the drives on the cable.

A controller's document refers to these indices to say which actuator drives which joint or wheel. For example, a Strider document for a 4-wheel base maps its wheels to the gateway's actuators [0, 1, 2, 3].

Motor units and joint units are defined in different documents:

Unit Where it is defined Motor (rpm, Nm, encoder counts) The gateway's actuator specification: gear ratio, torque and speed limits, encoder resolution Joint or wheel (rad, rad/s, m) The controller's document: kinematics, limits, and the mapping from actuators to joints

docs.title: Safety Behavior
docs.text:
• Watchdog. If a controller stops sending commands while the servo is on, the gateway keeps the last command for 3 s, then switches the servo off.
  • Limits. The gateway clamps velocity and torque commands to the actuator limits of its document. Position limits come from the controller's document.
  • Emergency stop. When a controller or the test console requests an emergency stop, the gateway sends a quick stop to the EtherCAT drives and switches the servo off. How the drives slow down depends on their quick stop settings. These software stops do not replace the hardware emergency stop (Stop Controls).
  • Fault reporting. Drive faults, lost communication and missing devices are reported in the gateway's Gateway events log with a hint about what to check (Running Nodes).
  • One hardware type per gateway. A gateway drives either real drives on one bus or one simulated robot. Use separate gateways for separate buses.

docs.title: Sensors and Cameras
docs.text:
Stellar Station has built-in gateways for the two sensors its navigation and walking controllers use: an RGB-D camera and an IMU. In simulation they read the cameras and IMUs of Isaac Sim. For real sensors, a small computer next to the sensors runs the Device Bridge, which serves real devices exactly as Isaac Sim serves simulated ones.

flowchart TB
    I["Isaac Sim + Isaac Bridge<br>(simulation)"]
    DB["Device Bridge<br>(real camera / IMU)"]
    I -- "TCP 53335" --> CG["Camera gateway"]
    DB -- "TCP 53335" --> CG
    I -- "TCP 53334" --> IG["IMU gateway"]
    DB -- "TCP 53334" --> IG
    CG --> VO["Visual odometry"]
    CG --> LOC["Localizer"]
    IG --> VO
    IG --> LEG["Legged locomotion"]
Your sensor Use A camera or IMU in Isaac Sim Camera gateway / IMU gateway, connected to Isaac Sim (this page) A real RGB-D camera (e.g. Intel RealSense) or USB IMU The Device Bridge on a sensor computer, plus the Camera gateway / IMU gateway Any other device (digital I/O, force sensors, custom hardware) Your own gateway module (Create Custom Modules)

docs.title: 1. Camera Gateway
docs.text:
Add the node with Add node › Gateway › Camera gateway and a name such as cam0. Nodes that use the camera connect to its camera port.

The camera gateway's inspector

docs.title: Connection
docs.text:
In the CAMERA GATEWAY section of the inspector:

Field Value Camera name The name of the camera: in Isaac Sim, the camera prim's name (for example cam0 for /World/jackal/links/base_link/cam0); with the Device Bridge, the bridge's robot name Camera host The address of the Isaac Sim computer or the sensor computer. The field is greyed out when a camera address is configured for the unit; the gateway then uses that address at every start, even if an uploaded YAML names another. To change it, contact Sodero support. Port 53335

docs.title: Camera Settings
docs.text:
Stop the node, change the values and click Save settings.

Setting Meaning fps Expected frame rate (the source decides the actual rate) frame id Name of the camera's optical frame, at most 15 characters, for example cam0_optical. The map bundle's extrinsics refer to this name. width, height Image size; 0 takes it from the frames Intrinsics fov mode with the horizontal field of view in degrees, or manual mode with fx, fy, cx, cy in pixels. A new camera gateway offers only the field of view; load manual values with Upload yaml (Device Bridge › Camera). Simulation camera Connection timeouts

Isaac Sim renders cameras with square pixels and the principal point at the image center, so fov mode with the camera's horizontal field of view is exact. Isaac Bridge prints each camera's field of view in the Isaac Sim console when the scene plays.

docs.title: See the Image
docs.text:
While the camera gateway runs, click Camera view on its node card:

Camera view of cam0: frame rate, frame age and resolution

docs.title: 2. IMU Gateway
docs.text:
Add the node with Add node › Gateway › IMU gateway. Nodes that use the IMU connect to its ports.

Setting Meaning Robot in World The robot whose IMU to read: its articulation prim name in Isaac Sim, or the Device Bridge's robot name Sample rate (Hz) IMU sample rate (default 250) Sensor event rate (Hz) Rate of the published IMU events (default 20)

The IMU gateway connects to the controller's configured simulator or sensor address. To set or change that address for your controller, contact Sodero support.

In Isaac Sim, a robot publishes IMU data when its robot prim names the link that carries the IMU in rc:imuLink (Robot Setup).

docs.title: 3. Mounting: Where the Sensor Sits
docs.text: Sensor data is in the sensor's own frame. Where the camera is mounted on the robot (its position and orientation relative to the robot's base_link) is part of the map bundle's extrinsics, used by the Localizer (Load and Configure a Map). Measure the mounting on the robot; do not rotate the data in the source.

docs.title: 4. Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix Camera log: Waiting for simulator at …:53335 (World not running?) Isaac Sim is not playing, the camera host is wrong, or a firewall blocks port 53335 Camera log: …publishes frames of camera(s) … but none of camera 'cam0' Camera name does not match a camera in the scene Camera log: Frames … are stale or carry capture times that do not match this Station's clock The clocks of the two computers differ. Synchronize them (NTP), or stop sending capture times at the source (Isaac Sim: start it with RC_CAMERA_CAPTURE_TIME=0; Device Bridge: send_capture_time: false) so that the Station uses arrival times. Camera view is black or frozen The camera prim looks at nothing, or the scene is paused

docs.title: Simulation Gateway
docs.text:
A simulation gateway is an actuator gateway of type Isaac Sim. Instead of a fieldbus it drives the joints of a robot in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, through the Isaac Bridge extension on the Isaac Sim computer. The controller connected to it (Motion Studio, Strider, Articulation) uses the same interface as with real motors, so its document and your applications carry over to the real robot. The real robot still needs its own checks: motor directions, gear ratios, encoders, limits and sensors.

flowchart TB
    subgraph SX ["Stellar X"]
        C["Controller"] -- servo_link --> G["Simulation gateway<br>Robot name: jackal"]
    end
    subgraph PC ["Isaac Sim computer"]
        B["Isaac Bridge"] --> R["/World/jackal<br>articulation"]
    end
    G -- "commands · TCP 53333" --> B
    B -- "joint states · TCP 53334" --> G

docs.title: 1. The Name Rule
docs.text:
The gateway's Robot name must be exactly the name of the robot's articulation prim in the Isaac Sim scene.

Isaac Bridge serves every articulation in the scene under the name of its prim: the robot at /World/jackal is served as jackal. A simulation gateway subscribes to the robot whose name equals its Robot name. If the names differ (Jackal vs. jackal, jackal_1 vs. jackal), the gateway never receives a joint state, keeps waiting and the robot never moves.

Station (gateway) Isaac Sim (scene) Robot name jackal Articulation prim /World/jackal Actuator 1, 2, 3, 4 (indices 0–3) The robot's 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th joint, in the order they are defined in the USD file DOF offset 0 The gateway starts at the robot's first joint

Use names with lowercase letters, digits and _, starting with a letter. Every robot in the scene must have a unique prim name.

docs.title: 2. Create a Simulation Gateway
docs.text:
1. Add an Actuator gateway node on the Station.
  2. Either import a simulation .gw (Import .gw), or click Edit Stellar Gateway Designer, choose Isaac Sim, and add one actuator per joint of the robot (Gateway Designer).

  3. In the node's TARGET section, click Change and set:

    • Robot name: the articulation prim name (see the rule above).
    • Sim host: the IP address of the Isaac Sim computer.

    Click Done. Changes take effect when the gateway starts next time.

Robot name and Sim host

If Sodero support has configured a default simulator address for your controller, the gateway connects to that address and Sim host is ignored.

docs.title: 3. Check the Connection
docs.text:
Start Isaac Sim's scene (Play), then start the gateway. Its Gateway events log shows:

Simulation: robot 'jackal', simulator at 192.168.60.20; waiting for it to start.
Simulator connected.
Log message Meaning waiting for it to start No joint state arrives yet. Normal until Isaac Sim plays. If it stays, see Troubleshooting. Simulator connected. Joint states arrive; the controller can switch the servo on. Simulator connection lost; servo turned OFF. The simulation stopped or the network dropped. The gateway reconnects by itself. Simulator connected again; turn the servo on to continue. Switch the servo on again in the controller UI.

When the simulation is stopped and played again, Isaac Sim puts the robot back at its starting pose, and the controller's servo is off until you switch it on again.

docs.title: 4. Several Robots and Shared Robots
docs.text:
• Several robots: add one gateway (and controller) per robot, each with its own Robot name. All of them use the same Isaac Sim computer and ports.
  • One robot, several gateways: an arm and its gripper can be driven by two gateways on the same articulation. Set the gripper gateway's DOF offset to the index of the gripper's first joint (Gateway Designer).

docs.title: 5. Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix The log stays at waiting for it to start Isaac Sim is not playing; Sim host is not the Isaac Sim computer; its firewall blocks TCP 53333–53334; Robot name does not match the prim name The Isaac Bridge window does not list the robot The prim has no articulation root (Robot Setup) The Isaac Bridge window shows the robot as not bound The robot is not a valid PhysX articulation (check the Isaac Sim console), or two prims share the name (Robot Setup) Servo on is accepted but the robot does not move Strider: the drive mode is not Twist. Motion Studio: the joint count of the scene differs from the gateway's actuators. A wheel or joint turns the wrong way The joint order or axis in the scene differs from the document.
