Fix the scene or the document; do not invert signs elsewhere. Motion looks slow, or localization lags The simulation runs slower than real time: controllers follow simulation time, but camera-based localization runs on wall-clock time. Lower the scene's physics and render rates, close other GPU programs (Real-Time Performance).

docs.title: Test Console
docs.text:
The test console moves the actuators of one actuator gateway without a robot controller. You switch the servo on and off, choose a drive mode, and send position, velocity or torque targets to each actuator. Use it to check the wiring, the directions, the gear ratios and the encoder settings of a gateway before a controller drives the robot. EtherCAT Mobile Base › Step 5 shows a complete test of four wheels in velocity mode.

Real motors move. Test one actuator at a time, with small values, with the mechanism free to move and the hardware emergency stop within reach. The console does not limit position targets, and its EMERGENCY STOP does not replace the hardware emergency stop (Stop Controls).

docs.title: Open the Test Console
docs.text:
The test console is for a gateway that no robot controller uses.

  1. Stop the robot controllers on the Station. The Station does not open a test while a Motion Studio node runs (a robot controller (CM) is running — stop the robot before opening the test console), and starting a robot controller (Motion Studio, Strider or Articulation) ends every running test.
  2. Select the gateway and click Start node. Test Stellar Gateway in its CONTROL section unlocks when the gateway runs.
  3. Click Test Stellar Gateway. The console opens in a new browser tab.
  4. If the console shows Gateway not connected, click Connect. The console always connects with the servo off.

While the test runs, the console is a node of the graph, sodero.actuator_test.NAME (NAME is the gateway's name), connected to the gateway's servo_link. It has a red dashed outline because it is not part of your saved graph; do not add it with Adopt running. The gateway's CONTROL section shows Open test console, which opens the console again, and Stop test.

① the test console, connected to the gateway's servo_link ② the gateway's test console buttons

docs.title: Screen Layout
docs.text:
① EMERGENCY STOP ② Servo ON and Servo OFF ③ the drive mode of all actuators ④ the target velocity of actuator 1 Area Description Top bar The gateway, and the connection: Gateway Connected, Gateway Disconnected, connecting… or Starting…. The theme menu and the deg / rad button change the display only. SERVER LOG Messages of the console's own connection to the gateway. The gateway's events, such as drive faults and Servo ON: all N drive(s) enabled., are in the gateway's LOGS › Gateway events on the Station page. EMERGENCY STOP ① Quick stop of every drive of the gateway, with the servo off. Click it again to release it, then click Servo ON. SERVO CMD ② Servo ON and Servo OFF for all actuators of the gateway; Fault Reset resets drive faults. After a fault reset, switch the servo off and on again. DRIVE MODE — APPLY TO ALL AXES ③ The drive mode of every actuator: POSITION, VELOCITY, TORQUE or IMPEDANCE. Apply sets it, sets every position target to the measured position and every velocity and torque target to zero. Trajectory ON On: a new position target is approached smoothly, in about 1 to 2 s. Off: the target is sent as a step. Actuator cards A1, A2, … One card per actuator, in the gateway's order (A1 is actuator 1, index 0): its own Drive Mode menu, the servo indicator Enable / Disable, the target sliders and the measured values Actual qa, Actual dqa and Actual taua.

Targets and measured values are at the joint, after the gear: degrees (or radians), degrees per second and newton-meters.

docs.title: Drive Modes
docs.text:
Mode Command When the actuator moves POSITION qa_d · Target Position, ±180° When you release the slider, the actuator moves to the new position. VELOCITY dqa_d · Target Velocity, ±180 °/s While you hold the slider. On release the target returns to 0. TORQUE taua_d · Torque Feedforward, ±10 Nm While you hold the slider. On release the target returns to 0. IMPEDANCE qa_d · Target Position, with the stiffness K (Nm/rad, 10 by default) and the damping D (Nm·s/rad, 0.5 by default) The actuator is pulled toward the target position like a spring with a damper. Enter K and D, then press Enter.

Only the slider of the actuator's drive mode commands it. The gateway limits velocity and torque commands to the limits of its document; position targets are not limited, so keep them inside the range the mechanism can move. In TORQUE mode nothing limits the speed: use small torques.

When a controller drives the gateway, it chooses the drive mode itself for each command. In the test console you choose it (EtherCAT Gateway › Process Data).

docs.title: Run a Test
docs.text:
1. Choose the drive mode under DRIVE MODE — APPLY TO ALL AXES and click Apply.
  2. Click Servo ON. Check the gateway's log on the Station page for Servo ON: all N drive(s) enabled. The cards show Enable as soon as the gateway accepts the request, so only the log line confirms that every drive is enabled.
  3. Move one actuator with a small value, and check its direction and travel against the measured value.
  4. When you are done, click Servo OFF.

docs.title: End the Test
docs.text:
1. Click Servo OFF in the console.
  2. Click Stop test in the gateway's CONTROL section. The test node leaves the graph.

Closing the console's tab does not end the test.

The console keeps sending the last command until you change it. If its tab closes or the network drops while an actuator moves, the actuator keeps moving. Open the console again with Open test console and click Servo OFF or EMERGENCY STOP, or press the hardware emergency stop. Stop test without Servo OFF leaves the last command active for up to 3 s, until the gateway's watchdog switches the servo off.

docs.title: Change the Gateway Document
docs.text:
The Station refuses to save a gateway document while the gateway runs and while its test is open. To change a value found in a test, for example a drive's polarity:

  1. Click Servo OFF in the console.
  2. Click Stop test in the gateway's CONTROL section.
  3. Click Stop node on the gateway.
  4. Change the document in the Gateway Designer, or import a new .gw.
  5. Click Start node on the gateway, then Test Stellar Gateway, and test again.

Stop the test before you stop the gateway. While the gateway is stopped, its CONTROL section shows no Stop test, and saves stay refused (Gateway '…' has a test console open). In that case, start the gateway again, click Stop test, and then stop the gateway.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause and fix The Station refuses to open the test: a robot controller (CM) is running …, or the console shows A controller is already running A Motion Studio node runs. Stop it, then click Connect in the console. The console shows Gateway not connected Click Connect. If it does not connect, check that the gateway is Operating. The cards show Enable, but the gateway's log shows Servo ON failed A drive did not enable. Check its STO and enable inputs, the emergency stop and its main power, then click Servo OFF and Servo ON. An actuator does not react to a slider The slider does not belong to the actuator's drive mode, or the servo is off. After EMERGENCY STOP is released, a drive does not enable again Click Servo ON. If the drive still does not enable, click Stop test, stop and start the gateway, and open the test again. The test ended by itself A robot controller was started on the Station.

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text: This page explains the building blocks you will meet everywhere in Stellar: the Station, nodes, ports, gateways, controllers and design documents. Read it once before the Quick Start; the rest of the documentation uses these terms without explaining them again.

docs.title: What Runs on Stellar X
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph SX ["Stellar X"]
        direction TB
        UI["Stellar Station<br>web page · port 80"]
        NS["Network Settings<br>web page · port 3000"]
        WS["SSH Workspace<br>ssh · port 2222"]
        RT["Real-time runtime<br>runs the Station's nodes"]
        UI --> RT
        WS --> RT
    end
    PC["Your PC<br>(browser, SSH, Isaac Sim)"] --> UI
    PC --> NS
    PC --> WS
    RT -- "EtherCAT" --> HW["Motors and drives"]
    RT -- "LAN" --> SIM["Isaac Sim<br>(simulated robot)"]
Part What it is Stellar Station The web page of the controller (http://ROBOT_ADDRESS). You build the robot system as a graph of nodes, load their documents, start them and watch their logs. Network Settings A small page on port 3000 for the LAN address and SSH keys. See Network Settings. SSH Workspace A development environment on the controller with the sodero command-line tool, for scripts and AI coding agents. See SSH Workspace. Runtime Runs the Station's nodes in real time.

docs.title: Station and Nodes
docs.text:
A Station is the complete robot system on one controller. It is a graph of nodes: each node is one program, such as a motor gateway, a robot controller, a camera or your own application.

When you click Add node on the Station page, you choose one of four node types:

Type Purpose Built-in modules Gateway Connects simulation or hardware to the system Actuator gateway, IMU gateway, Camera gateway Controller Defines a robot unit and its control Motion Studio, Strider, Articulation, Legged locomotion, Localizer, Visual odometry, Navigator Compound Combines several robot units into one system Your own compound modules Application Defines robot behaviors and task logic Your own modules

Most built-in nodes have an ID of the form sodero.<kind>.<name>. You choose the name; the kind comes from the module:

Module Node ID Actuator gateway sodero.actuator_gateway.NAME Camera gateway sodero.camera_gateway.NAME IMU gateway sodero.imu_gateway.NAME Motion Studio sodero.mmc.NAME Strider sodero.mlc.NAME Articulation sodero.amc.NAME Legged locomotion rc.legged_locomotion.NAME Visual odometry, Localizer, Navigator sodero.visual_odometry, sodero.localizer, sodero.navigator (one of each per Station)

docs.title: Ports and Connections
docs.text:
Nodes work together through ports. Every node card on the Station page lists two kinds:

  • REQUIRES: a service the node needs from another node.
  • PROVIDES: a service the node offers to other nodes.

You connect a required port to a compatible provided port by dragging between them. The most important connection is the servo link between a controller and its gateway:

flowchart TB
    S["Strider<br>sodero.mlc.jackal"] -- "servo_link" --> G["Actuator gateway<br>sodero.actuator_gateway.jackal"]
    G -- "simulation" --> I["Isaac Sim<br>robot 'jackal'"]
    G -. "or EtherCAT" .-> M["Real motors"]
From (requires) To (provides) Meaning Motion Studio, Strider, Articulation servo_link Actuator gateway servo_link The controller drives the gateway's actuators Localizer camera Camera gateway camera The localizer sees through this camera Localizer odometry Strider odometry (or Visual odometry) The localizer follows the robot's motion Navigator localization, map Localizer localization, map Where the robot is, and the map to plan on Navigator mobile_base Strider mobile_base The base the navigator drives Legged locomotion imu IMU gateway imu Body orientation for walking

The Station only connects compatible ports, so a wrong connection is refused at once instead of failing later.

docs.title: Gateways: Simulation or Real Hardware
docs.text:
A gateway is the only node that talks to actuators. Controllers never touch hardware directly; they send commands through their gateway. That is why the same controller and controller document can drive a simulated robot and a real one: the gateway's document decides which. The real robot still needs its own checks of actuator mapping, calibration, limits and sensors.

Hardware type of the .gw Drives Isaac Sim A robot in NVIDIA Isaac Sim on a PC on the same network, through the Isaac Bridge extension EtherCAT Real EtherCAT drives on the controller's EtherCAT port

Names must match. A simulation gateway finds its robot in Isaac Sim by name. The gateway's Robot name must be exactly the name of the robot's articulation prim in the Isaac Sim scene (for example /World/jackal for the robot name jackal). With a different name, the gateway keeps waiting and the robot never moves. See Simulation Gateway.

docs.title: Design Documents
docs.text:
Actuator gateways and robot controllers are configured by a design document. You create documents with Stellar Designer (gateway documents with its Gateway Designer) and load them into nodes on the Station page.

File Node Contents .gw Actuator gateway Hardware type, actuators, EtherCAT or simulation settings .sdd Motion Studio Manipulator: kinematics, dynamics, actuator mapping .sddm Strider Mobile base: drive type, wheels, limits, actuator mapping .sdda Articulation Articulated robot: joints and actuator mapping

Camera and IMU gateways, visual odometry, the localizer, the navigator and legged locomotion have no design document. They have settings that you edit in the node's inspector on the Station page (Design Documents). The localizer and the navigator also use a map bundle (.nav): one file with the map of the site and their settings (Load and Configure a Map).

Your own programs are installed as modules (packages) on the Modules page and run as nodes on the Station.

docs.title: Simulation First, Then Real
docs.text:
The recommended workflow follows the same order every time:

  1. Design the robot in Stellar Designer (.sdd, .sddm or .sdda).
  2. Simulate: add a simulation gateway and the controller on the Station, connect them, and drive the robot in Isaac Sim.
  3. Go real: give the robot an EtherCAT gateway document for its drives. The controller, its document and your applications are reused. Before you operate the robot, verify the actuator mapping, calibration, limits and sensor settings on the hardware, as in EtherCAT Mobile Base.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning Station The robot system on one controller, shown as a node graph on the Station page Node One program in the Station, such as a gateway, a controller, a sensor or your module Port A connection point of a node: REQUIRES (needs) or PROVIDES (offers) Gateway A node that connects controllers to actuators or sensors, real or simulated Controller A node that controls a robot unit: Motion Studio, Strider, Articulation, Legged locomotion Design document The configuration file of an actuator gateway or a robot controller: .gw, .sdd, .sddm, .sdda Map bundle A .nav file with the map of a site and the settings of the localizer and the navigator Module A program that runs as a node: built in, or your own package installed on the Modules page SDR A backup file of the whole Station: graph, documents and settings World The simulated scene in Isaac Sim that the Station's simulation gateways connect to Isaac Bridge The Isaac Sim extension that connects the World to the Station

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
Updated example pair (2026-10-27)

Download both the .gw and .sddm files from this page again if you have older copies. They use the current sodero.* node IDs; older screenshots may still show rc.*. See Compatibility and Downloads.

You will build a small robot system on Stellar X and drive a simulated Clearpath Jackal in NVIDIA Isaac Sim with Strider. It takes about 15 minutes once Stellar X is on your network and Isaac Sim with the Isaac Bridge extension is installed (see Before You Start). You will:

  1. add an actuator gateway and a Strider controller on Stellar Station,
  2. load their design documents,
  3. connect Isaac Sim, and
  4. jog the robot from the browser.
flowchart TB
    B["Your browser<br>Stellar Station · Strider"]
    subgraph SX ["Stellar X"]
        S["Strider<br>sodero.mlc.jackal"] -- servo_link --> G["Actuator gateway<br>sodero.actuator_gateway.jackal"]

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text: You need Details Stellar X Powered on and reachable from your PC (Stellar X › Network Configuration, Network Settings). In this guide its address is 192.168.60.18, an example address on a lab network; use your controller's address instead, for example 10.0.0.1 on a direct cable. A PC with NVIDIA Isaac Sim Isaac Sim 6.0 with the Isaac Bridge 1.0.0 extension installed and enabled (Isaac Bridge Installation), on the same network as Stellar X. In this guide its address is 192.168.60.20. Example files jackal.gw (gateway), jackal.sddm (Strider) and jackal_warehouse.zip (Isaac Sim scene, 6 MB). Download all three and extract the scene.

docs.title: Step 1: Add the Gateway
docs.text:
1. Open http://192.168.60.18 in your browser.

  2. Click Add node, choose Gateway ①, then Actuator gateway ② and click Next ③.

    Gateway › Actuator gateway

  3. Name it jackal ① and click Add node ②.

docs.title: Step 2: Load the Gateway Document
docs.text:
1. Select the new node sodero.actuator_gateway.jackal. In its inspector, click the upload icon in DEFINITION (Import .gw).

  2. On From your PC ①, choose jackal.gw ② and click Import ③.

  3. In TARGET, click Change and set the two values:

    • Robot name: jackal. It must equal the robot's prim name in Isaac Sim (/World/jackal).
    • Sim host: the IP address of your Isaac Sim PC.

    Click Done.

If the robot name differs from the prim name in Isaac Sim, the gateway waits forever and the robot never moves.

docs.title: Step 3: Add Strider and Connect It
docs.text:
1. Click Add node, choose Controller ① › Strider ② and click Next ③. Name it jackal and click Add node.

  2. Select sodero.mlc.jackal and click the upload icon in DEFINITION (Import .sddm). On From your PC ①, choose jackal.sddm ② and click Import ③.

  3. Connect the two nodes: drag from the Strider's servo_link (left edge) to the gateway's servo_link (right edge), or click Auto-connect next to servo_link in the Strider's inspector.

The gateway and Strider connected through servo_link

docs.title: Step 4: Play the Scene in Isaac Sim
docs.text:
1. Open jackal_warehouse.usd in Isaac Sim (File › Open). The scene contains a Clearpath Jackal at /World/jackal and a Clearpath Dingo at /World/dingo_d in a warehouse.
  2. Press Play.
  3. Open Window › Isaac Bridge. It shows the ports as serving and jackal … bound, 4 DOF.
Isaac Bridge status: ① ports serving ② robots bound ③ cameras ④ Rescan

The Isaac Sim PC must accept TCP connections from Stellar X on ports 53333–53335. Allow them in its firewall (Isaac Bridge Installation).

Tip: To use your own robot instead, prepare its scene as described in Robot Setup: its articulation prim name is its robot name, and its joints, in order, are the gateway's actuators.

Tip: If you will continue with Navigate in Simulation, start Isaac Sim with the camera setting of its Step 1 now. Then you do not need to restart Isaac Sim later.

docs.title: Step 5: Start the Nodes
docs.text:
1. Select the gateway and click Start node. Wait until its state is Operating.
  2. Select the Strider and click Start node.

In the gateway's LOGS (stream Gateway events) you see the connection to Isaac Sim:

Gateway sodero.actuator_gateway.jackal starting: simulation, 4 actuator(s), 1.0 ms cycle.
Simulation: robot 'jackal', simulator at 192.168.60.20; waiting for it to start.
Simulator connected.

docs.title: Step 6: Jog the Robot with Strider
docs.text:
1. In the Strider node's inspector, click Strider in CONTROL. Strider opens in a new tab.
  2. Open the Drive page (gamepad icon in the left rail).
  3. Under Drive Mode, click Twist ①.
  4. Under Servo / Safety, switch Servo On ②.
  5. Press and hold Forward (W) on the pad ⑤. The robot drives while you hold the button and stops when you release it. Turn Left (A), Turn Right (D) and Backward (S) work the same way.
Strider's Drive page: ① Twist ② Servo On ③ Live switch for the keyboard ④ speed limits ⑤ drive pad ⑥⑦ stop and emergency stop ⑧ readiness

Tip: Switch on Live ③ in Manual Drive to drive with the keyboard: W/S forward and back, A/D turn, Space stops.

The simulated Jackal after a short drive and turn

When you are done, switch the servo off and click Idle under Drive Mode.

docs.title: One Platform from Design to the Real Robot
docs.text:
Sodero connects robot design, simulation and operation on one controller. You describe the robot in Stellar Designer, run it on Stellar X with the built-in controllers, and drive it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim or on real motors through a gateway.

The same controller and application structure can be reused in simulation and on supported hardware. Before operating the physical robot, configure its gateway and verify actuator mapping, calibration, limits and sensor settings.

docs.title: Core Architecture
docs.text:
Gateways separate controllers from hardware. Controllers never talk to hardware directly. A gateway connects them to EtherCAT drives, to a robot in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, or to sensors, so the same controller and controller document can drive a simulated robot and a real one.

One Station for every node. Gateways, controllers, navigation and your own modules run as nodes of one Station on Stellar X. They are connected through ports with defined interfaces, so built-in nodes and your own work together in the same way on every robot.

docs.title: From Design to the Real Robot
docs.text:
The Sodero ecosystem connects the entire process, from robot design and validation to physical deployment, into a single pipeline.

flowchart TB
    D["Design<br>Stellar Designer"] --> S["Compose<br>Stellar Station"]
    S --> V["Simulate<br>Isaac Sim + Isaac Bridge"]
    V --> R["Run<br>Stellar X + real hardware"]
    R -. "same controller,<br>EtherCAT gateway" .- V

Design: Stellar Designer. A web-based tool for defining your robot's kinematics, links, joints, wheels and actuator mapping, and the gateway that connects its actuators, without any hardware.

Compose: Stellar Station. The control center on the controller. Add gateways and controllers as nodes, connect their ports, load their design documents and start them, all in the browser.

Simulate: NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The Isaac Bridge extension connects a robot in Isaac Sim to the Station. The simulated robot is driven by the same controller and controller document as the real one, through a simulation gateway instead of an EtherCAT gateway.

Run: Stellar X. The motion controller with an EtherCAT master that runs the Station and its nodes. On the real robot, its EtherCAT gateway drives the servo drives, after you have checked the actuator mapping, calibration and limits on the hardware.

In simulation and on the real robot alike, you operate the robot from the same built-in controller UIs: Motion Studio for manipulators, Strider for mobile bases and Articulation for articulated and legged robots.

Tip: Every tool runs in the browser and is served by Stellar X itself. Connect a PC to the controller's network and open its address; there is nothing to install on your PC except Isaac Sim and the Isaac Bridge extension for simulation.

Sodero Cloud. The same Stellar Station, design documents and controller UIs also run in Sodero Cloud, where robots are simulated in Robot Worlds in the browser instead of Isaac Sim on your PC. See the Sodero Cloud manual.

docs.title: Integration and Extensibility
docs.text:
Beyond controlling a single robot, Sodero fits into complex system integration (SI) environments.

Modules. Package your own programs and install them on the Station. They run as nodes next to the built-in ones and use the same interfaces to command robots, read sensors and send navigation goals.

SSH Workspace and the sodero CLI. Every Station operation is available as a command that prints JSON, for scripts, CI pipelines and AI coding agents.

docs.title: What's New in 2.0
docs.text:
Version 2.0 turns Stellar X from a single-robot motion controller into a complete robot system on one controller:

  • Stellar Station: build the robot system as a graph of nodes (gateways, controllers, sensors, navigation and your own modules) and run it from the browser.
  • One Stellar Designer for every design document: manipulators (.sdd), mobile bases (.sddm), articulated robots (.sdda) and gateways (.gw).
  • Mobile robots and navigation: Strider drives wheeled bases; the Localizer and Navigator add map-based localization and autonomous navigation.
  • Isaac Bridge: connect robots in NVIDIA Isaac Sim to the Station over the network, with cameras and IMUs.
  • SSH Workspace and AI agents: develop on the controller over SSH and let AI coding agents operate the Station with the sodero CLI.

Continue with Key Concepts, then try the Quick Start.

docs.title: Network Settings
docs.text:
Stellar X serves a small settings page on port 3000. Use it for the two things you need before anything else:

  • the IP address of the controller's LAN port Eth1, and
  • SSH access to the controller's SSH workspace.

Open the page from any computer on the same network:

http://ROBOT_ADDRESS:3000

In this guide the controller's address is 192.168.60.18, an example address on a lab network, so the page is http://192.168.60.18:3000. Replace it with your controller's address.

Initial address: static 10.0.0.1. Eth1 starts with the static address 10.0.0.1 (subnet mask 255.255.255.0). To reach it the first time, connect your PC with a cable and give the PC a static address in the same subnet, such as 10.0.0.2 (Stellar X). Then open http://10.0.0.1:3000 and change the address under IP Configuration.

The page needs no sign-in: anyone on the same network can change the address and register SSH keys. Connect Stellar X only to networks you trust.

The Network Settings page

Stellar Station itself is served on the standard web port: http://ROBOT_ADDRESS (port 80). Port 3000 is only for these settings.

docs.title: 1. IP Configuration
docs.text:
The IP CONFIGURATION card shows and changes the address of Eth1. The page shows no port name; every value on the card belongs to Eth1.

Current address and IP assignment No. Item Description 1 Current address The address Eth1 has now, how it got it (DHCP or Static), the subnet mask and the port's MAC address. Connected means a cable is plugged in and the link is up. 2 DHCP The router assigns the address. This is the simplest setup on an office or lab network. 3 Static You enter the address yourself. Use it for a direct cable between your PC and the controller, or on a network without a DHCP server. 4 Apply Applies the selection. Nothing changes until you click it.

docs.title: Set a Static Address
docs.text:
Static address
  1. Click Static ①. The card shows IP ADDRESS and SUBNET MASK.
  2. Enter the new address in IP ADDRESS ②. The subnet mask ③ is fixed to 255.255.255.0.
  3. Click Apply ④.

After Apply, the controller moves to the new address and the page stops answering at the old one. Open http://NEW_ADDRESS:3000 to continue.

Your PC must be on the same subnet to reach the new address. For example, after setting 10.0.0.1 on a direct cable, give your PC a static address such as 10.0.0.2 with mask 255.255.255.0.

Automatic rollback. If the new setting cannot be applied, or no address comes up (for example DHCP is selected but no DHCP server answers), the controller restores its previous settings by itself and the page reports what happened.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The page changes Eth1 only. Eth2 keeps using DHCP. The EtherCAT port is reserved for EtherCAT devices; it never gets an IP address and is not shown here (Stellar X › Device Overview).
  • No default gateway is configured. Stellar X works on the local network and does not need Internet access.
  • With DHCP, find the controller's address in your router's client list; its host name is stellar-x.

docs.title: 2. SSH Access
docs.text:
The SSH ACCESS card controls who can sign in to the controller's SSH workspace. The workspace accepts SSH keys only; there is no password sign-in.

SSH workspace status, registered keys and key registration No. Item Description 1 Connection command The exact command to connect, with Copy. Running means the workspace is up. 2 Operating system Shows the key command for Windows (PowerShell) or macOS · Linux. 3 Key command Creates a key on your computer if it has none, then prints its public key. 4 Public key box Paste the printed line here. It starts with ssh-ed25519. 5 Add key Registers the key. It appears under REGISTERED KEYS.

docs.title: Register a Computer
docs.text:
1. Select your operating system ②, click Copy ③ and run the command in a terminal on your computer.

    macOS · LinuxWindows (PowerShell) 
    [ -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub ] || { mkdir -p ~/.ssh && ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519; }; cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

    if (!(Test-Path $HOME\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub)) { mkdir $HOME\.ssh -Force | Out-Null; ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f $HOME\.ssh\id_ed25519 }; Get-Content $HOME\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub | Set-Clipboard; Get-Content $HOME\.ssh\id_ed25519.pub

    On Windows the command also copies the key to the clipboard. When ssh-keygen asks for a passphrase, press Enter twice to create the key without one.

  2. Paste the printed line into the box ④ and click Add key ⑤.

  3. Click Copy next to the connection command ① and run it:

    ssh -p 2222 sodero@192.168.60.18

To revoke access, click the trash icon next to a key under REGISTERED KEYS. The computer can no longer sign in; files in the workspace are kept.

Paste only the public key (the .pub file). The page refuses private keys and keys with options.

Each person or computer should have its own key. The key's comment (for example user@laptop) is shown in the list, so you can tell the keys apart.

Continue with SSH Workspace to learn what you can do once you are connected.

docs.title: Stellar X
docs.text: This guide takes you from unboxing and hardware assembly to the first network connection between Stellar X and your PC.

docs.title: 1. What's in the Box
docs.text:
Check that your package includes the following components. If anything is missing, contact our support team.

Stellar X Main Unit 24V Power Adapter Power Cable

docs.title: 2. Device Overview
docs.text:
The network and power ports are on the rear panel.

Rear panel: ① Eth1 ② Eth2 ③ EtherCAT Out ④ 24V DC In Port Initial setting How to change it Use 1. Eth1 Static address 10.0.0.1, subnet mask 255.255.255.0 On the Network Settings page: DHCP or another static address First connection with a cable from your PC; afterwards your office or lab network 2. Eth2 DHCP Not changed by the Network Settings page A router or switch that assigns addresses by DHCP 3. EtherCAT Out No IP address — EtherCAT master output. Connect it to the IN port of the first EtherCAT drive. 4. 24V DC In — — Power input

docs.title: 3. Hardware Setup & Power On
docs.text:
Follow these steps in order to prevent electrical damage.

  1. Prepare the Adapter: Connect the power cable to the 24V power adapter. Do not plug it into the wall outlet yet.

  2. Connect to Stellar X: Insert the adapter's output cable into the 24V DC In port on the unit.

    To prevent electrical arcing (sparks) or connection issues, always connect the cable to the Stellar X unit first, and then plug the power adapter into the wall.

    The connector has a small guide notch inside. If it doesn't slide in easily, gently rotate the cable until the notch aligns with the port.

    Aligning the connector notch

  3. Secure the Connection: Once the connector is fully inserted, hand-tighten its metal nut so that it stays locked in place.

    Securing the locking nut

  4. Power Up: Plug the power cable into a wall outlet. Stellar X powers on automatically and takes about 1 minute to start up.

docs.title: 4. Network Configuration
docs.text:
Your PC must be on the same subnet as Stellar X.

  1. Physical Connection: Connect an Ethernet (LAN) cable to Eth1 (Port 1) on the Stellar X unit and the other end to your PC's LAN port.

    Connecting to Eth1

  2. Configure Your PC: Eth1 starts with the static address 10.0.0.1, so set your PC to a static IP in the same subnet (e.g., 10.0.0.2).

    Avoid using 10.0.0.1 for your PC, as this will cause an IP conflict.

    • For Ubuntu Users:

      1. Go to Settings > Network.
      2. Click the gear icon next to your wired connection.
      3. Select the IPv4 tab and choose Manual.
      4. Set Address: 10.0.0.2 / Netmask: 255.255.255.0.
      5. Click Apply.

    • For Windows Users:

      1. Go to Settings > Network & Internet > Ethernet.
      2. Find IP assignment and click Edit.
      3. Select Manual, toggle IPv4 On, and enter:
        • IP address: 10.0.0.2
        • Subnet mask: 255.255.255.0
      4. Click Save.

  3. Verify the Connection: Open your preferred web browser (Chrome, Edge, etc.) and type the following into the address bar: http://10.0.0.1

  4. Success! If Stellar Station appears, you are ready to start your project. Continue with the Quick Start.

    Stellar Station with an example robot system

    To change Eth1's address or to connect it to your office network, use the Network Settings page on port 3000. The rest of this documentation uses the example address 192.168.60.18 for Stellar X; replace it with your controller's address, for example 10.0.0.1 while you use the direct cable.

docs.title: Stop Controls
docs.text:
A robot on Stellar X can be stopped in several ways: buttons in the controller UIs and the test console, automatic stops of the gateway, and the emergency stop that you wire yourself. This page compares them, so that you know what each one does before real motors move.

On-screen buttons are not emergency stops. They are software functions of the controllers and the gateway, and they act only while the browser, the network, Stellar X and the drives work. Every robot with real motors needs a hardware emergency stop that removes motor power or triggers the drives' safe torque off (STO), wired as the drive manufacturer describes. Keep it within reach whenever the motors are powered.

docs.title: 1. Hardware Emergency Stop and STO
docs.text: The hardware emergency stop and the drives' STO inputs are part of your machine, not of Stellar X. How they stop the motors depends on your wiring and on the drives. While they are active, the drives cannot be enabled: the gateway reports Servo ON failed: drive … did not enable (EtherCAT Gateway › Troubleshooting). After you release them, switch the servo on again in the UI.

docs.title: 2. Stops in the UIs
docs.text:
Control What it does Servo afterwards To continue E-STOP (Strider, top bar) Cancels manual driving and the navigation goal and sets the wheel speeds to zero at once. The drives stay enabled and hold zero speed. The stop latches. On Clear E-Stop (the base switches to Idle), then Twist Stop Motion, Stop (Space), releasing a pad button (Strider, Drive page) Ends manual driving (and, for Stop Motion, a navigation goal). The base slows down at the acceleration limits of its document. On Drive again Releasing a jog button or Hold to move (Motion Studio) The arm slows down over a short ramp and holds its position. On — Stop (Articulation, top bar) Switches the servo off and latches a stop. Off Clear stop, then Servo on Servo Off / Servo off / Servo OFF (Strider, Motion Studio, Articulation, test console) Disables the drives. The motors no longer hold: a base rolls out, and a joint without a brake can fall. Whether a motor brake engages depends on the drive's configuration. Off Switch the servo on EMERGENCY STOP (test console) Sends a quick stop to every drive of the gateway and switches the servo off. How a drive slows down depends on its quick stop settings. While it is active, Servo ON and Fault Reset have no effect. Off Click it again to release it, then Servo ON. If a drive does not enable again, end the test and restart the gateway.

Motion Studio has no on-screen emergency stop. Use the hardware emergency stop, or switch the servo off where the arm can safely lose its holding torque.

A closed tab does not stop the robot. Closing a UI tab or losing the network connection is not a stop command. Strider stops manual driving within about a second, but a navigation goal continues. In Motion Studio and the test console, a motion that is running when the browser loses the page can continue. Stop the motion before you leave a UI, and use the hardware emergency stop when a UI does not respond.

docs.title: 3. Automatic Stops
docs.text: Situation What happens To continue A controller stops sending commands while the servo is on The gateway keeps the last command for 3 s, then switches the servo off (No commands from the robot controller for 3.0 s: servo turned OFF for safety.). Start the controller and switch the servo on EtherCAT communication is lost The gateway switches the servo off and reports EtherCAT communication lost. Fix the cable or the drive's power, then restart the gateway A drive reports a fault The gateway reports the fault in Gateway events. Fix the cause, Fault Reset or Error Reset, then switch the servo on Motion Studio: a joint limit, a speed or torque limit, or a collision Protective stop: the arm holds its position with the servo on (Manipulator › Robot System Parameters). Error Reset Motion Studio: no feedback from the gateway, or a critical drive fault Emergency stop: the controller requests a quick stop and the servo switches off. Stop and start the Motion Studio node Articulation: feedback older than 100 ms, or no new target for 200 ms The servo switches off and a stop latches. Clear stop, then Servo on Strider: no manual command for about 1 s The base slows to a stop. Drive again

docs.title: 4. Before You Power Real Motors
docs.text:
1. Wire and test the hardware emergency stop and the drives' STO.
  2. Lift wheels off the ground, or keep the axes clear of their end stops.
  3. Check each actuator alone with the test console, at low speed.
  4. Start the controller with low limits, and keep someone at the emergency stop.

docs.title: Create a Map from Your Site
Create a Map from Your Site
docs.text:
Stellar Station does not build maps on the robot; there is no SLAM. You make the map bundle of your site beforehand, from a 3D model or a 3D scan of the site, and then upload it as described in Load and Configure a Map. Every file and key of the bundle is specified in Map Bundle Format.

The Localizer matches the camera's depth images against the 3D point cloud of the bundle to find the robot on the map. The Navigator plans paths on the 2D occupancy grid. Both describe the same site in the same coordinates.

Any point-cloud tool, such as CloudCompare or Open3D, can do the steps below.

docs.title: 1. Choose the Coordinate Frames
docs.text:
Frame Meaning map The site: x and y horizontal, z up, the floor at z = 0, in meters. The point cloud, the grid, the initial pose and goals use it. odom Continuous motion measured by odometry (Strider wheel odometry or Visual odometry). It drifts; the Localizer corrects the drift. base_link The robot, on the floor: x forward, y left, z up. Camera optical frame, for example cam0_optical x right, y down, z forward along the view. 
flowchart TB
    M["map"] -- "Localizer<br>(drift correction)" --> O["odom"]
    O -- "odometry<br>(Strider or Visual odometry)" --> B["base_link<br>(on the floor)"]
    B -- "extrinsics.yaml<br>(fixed)" --> C["cam0_optical<br>(x right, y down, z forward)"]

The Localizer is planar by default (icp.planar: true): it estimates x, y and yaw of base_link and holds its height, roll and pitch at zero. base_link therefore lies on the floor, and the camera height in extrinsics.yaml is its height above the floor.

Measure the camera's x and y from the base origin that your odometry tracks, but its z from the floor, even when your robot model places base_link higher, for example at the wheel axles. A height taken from a raised base puts every camera point too low by that offset: the fit error exceeds icp.max_rmse and the localization status stays Initializing (initializing).

docs.title: 2. Get a Point Cloud
docs.text:
Choose the map frame first: x and y horizontal, z up, the floor at z = 0, in meters. Then collect points on every surface the camera will see:

  • 3D model: sample points on the surfaces of the site's model, for example the USD world of your Isaac Sim scene, with normals and colors where available. When the map frame is the world frame, poses in the simulator and on the map are the same.
  • 3D scan: scan the real site with a laser scanner or by photogrammetry, and level the scan so that the floor lies at z = 0.

docs.title: 3. Clean and Export the PLY
docs.text:
1. Remove people, vehicles and other objects that move, stray points and everything outside the site.
  2. Downsample to a point spacing of 2 to 5 cm, at most 2 million points; the Localizer reduces the map to map.voxel_size (5 cm by default) anyway.
  3. Export a binary little-endian PLY with float x, y, z, optional normals and uchar colors: points only, no faces and no extra fields (Point Cloud).

docs.title: 4. Make the Occupancy Grid
docs.text:
1. Pick the resolution (typically 0.05 m) and a rectangle that covers the cloud with a margin. Its lower-left corner is the origin; width and height are its size divided by the resolution, rounded up.
  2. Mark a cell occupied (0) when it holds points in the height band the robot can hit, from just above the floor to just above the robot, for example 0.05 to 0.65 m.
  3. Mark a cell free (254) when it holds floor points and no obstacle, and every other cell unknown (205).
  4. Write the PGM with its top row at the largest y, then the grid YAML (Occupancy Grid). Record the height band in meta.yaml as z_slice.

Tip: Compare the PGM with a top view of the point cloud. The walls must line up; a grid mirrored top to bottom was written bottom row first.

docs.title: 5. Write the YAML Files
docs.text:
Choose a map ID, name the three map files after it, and write the five YAML files: meta.yaml, localizer.yaml, navigator.yaml, extrinsics.yaml and initial_pose.yaml (Files). Copy the width, height, resolution and origin of the grid into meta.yaml without rounding.

Start navigator.yaml from the file of a working bundle, such as the warehouse example of Navigate in Simulation, and change values only.

docs.title: 6. Measure the Camera Mounting
docs.text: Measure the camera's optical center from base_link: x forward and y left from the base origin, z up from the floor. Measure its downward tilt and take the quaternion from extrinsics.yaml. Set camera_frame_id and the edge's child to the camera node's frame_id.

docs.title: 7. Pack the Bundle
docs.text:
# build/site.nav/ holds the five YAML files and map/
tar -czf site.nav.tgz -C build site.nav   # file for the Station page
cp site.nav.tgz site.nav                  # the same file, named for sodero maps upload
tar -tzf site.nav                         # every entry starts with site.nav/

Do not pack with tar -czf site.nav.tgz -C build/site.nav .: the ./ entry it adds is refused. Archive entries with hidden names, such as files some archivers add on macOS, are refused too.

docs.title: 8. Check the Bundle
docs.text:
The Station page checks the archive's layout when you upload it. The CLI preview checks every rule of the format without changing anything, so preview a new bundle from the SSH workspace first:

sodero navigation get --node sodero.localizer                           # note "sha256"
sodero maps upload site.nav --node sodero.localizer --if-sha256 SHA256  # preview only, without --execute

The preview reports the first problem it finds (Validation Errors).

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• The map frame has the floor at z = 0, and the point cloud and the grid use the same coordinates.
  • The grid files are map/MAP_ID.pgm and map/MAP_ID.yaml, and meta.yaml repeats their width, height, resolution and origin exactly.
  • The PLY holds only x, y, z with optional normals and colors, and at most 2 million points.
  • The grid YAML has exactly six keys, negate is 0 or 1, and free_thresh is below occupied_thresh.
  • camera_frame_id matches the camera node's frame_id, the edges use quat [x, y, z, w], and the camera height is measured from the floor.
  • initial_pose.yaml gives the pose of base_link, with yaw in radians.
  • navigator.yaml is complete, with your robot's robot_radius and speed limits.
  • The archive is a gzip tar with one top folder, at most 64 MiB, and the CLI preview reports no problem.
  • In simulation, the localization status reaches Healthy and the robot reaches a nearby goal before you drive the real robot.

Then upload the bundle: Load and Configure a Map.

docs.title: Load and Configure a Map
docs.text:
A map bundle (.nav) is one file that carries the map of one site together with the settings to localize and navigate in it. You upload it once to the Localizer; the Navigator uses the same bundle, and Visual odometry uses its camera calibration. This page loads a finished bundle, checks the values for the first run and starts the nodes.

You want to Page Load a finished bundle, such as the warehouse example This page Make a bundle for your own site Create a Map from Your Site Look up every file, key and message of the format Map Bundle Format

Stellar Station does not build maps on the robot; there is no SLAM. A bundle is made beforehand from a 3D model or a 3D scan of the site.

docs.title: 1. What You Need
docs.text:
• The bundle file, for example warehouse.nav.tgz of Navigate in Simulation. The Station page accepts names ending in .tgz; the CLI needs a name ending in .nav. Both are the same gzip-compressed tar, so you can copy site.nav.tgz to site.nav.
  • A Localizer node (sodero.localizer) and, to drive to goals, a Navigator node (sodero.navigator), connected as in Localization and Navigation › Set Up Navigation.

The bundle contains five settings files and three map files:

File Contents Read by meta.yaml The map ID and a description of the grid Localizer and Navigator localizer.yaml Localizer settings, including the point-cloud file Localizer navigator.yaml Navigator settings: robot size, speeds, tolerances Navigator extrinsics.yaml Where the camera is mounted on the robot Localizer and Visual odometry initial_pose.yaml The starting pose of the robot on the map Localizer map/MAP_ID.ply, .pgm, .yaml The 3D point cloud and the 2D occupancy grid of the site Localizer; Navigator and the map views

docs.title: 2. Upload the Bundle
docs.text: The Localizer and the Navigator share one bundle, so one upload to the Localizer serves both.

docs.title: Station Page
docs.text:
1. Stop the Localizer and the nodes that use its bundle (Navigator, Visual odometry).
  2. Select the Localizer node. In the inspector's LOCALIZER section, click Upload .nav and choose site.nav.tgz.
  3. The section shows the file name, and NAVIGATION SETTINGS lists the settings of the bundle.

The page checks the archive's layout. The CLI preview below checks every rule of the format, so preview a bundle you built yourself with the CLI before you upload it on the page.

docs.title: sodero CLI
docs.text:
sodero runtime node stop sodero.navigator --execute
sodero runtime node stop sodero.localizer --execute
sodero navigation get --node sodero.localizer                                     # note "sha256"
sodero maps upload site.nav --node sodero.localizer --if-sha256 SHA256            # preview: checks the bundle
sodero maps upload site.nav --node sodero.localizer --if-sha256 SHA256 --execute  # attach it
sodero runtime node start sodero.localizer --execute
sodero runtime node start sodero.navigator --execute
  • With Visual odometry, also stop sodero.visual_odometry before the upload, and start it again before the Localizer.
  • The file name must end in .nav, and the file may be at most 64 MiB.
  • The preview reports the first problem it finds (Validation Errors) and changes nothing.
  • After each upload or settings change, read the SHA-256 again before the next one.

Uploading a bundle replaces all of its settings, including changes saved on the Station page or with the CLI. Copy those changes into your files before you upload a new version.

docs.title: 3. Check the Values for the First Run
docs.text:
A bundle made for another robot needs your robot's values. Check these before the first run:

Value Setting Group in NAVIGATION SETTINGS Robot size robot_radius of local_costmap and global_costmap (the same value in both) Navigator Speeds FollowPath.desired_linear_vel (cruise speed), FollowPath.max_angular_vel (turn rate), velocity_smoother.max_velocity Navigator Camera mounting xyz and quat of the edge from base_link to the camera; the height is measured from the floor Camera calibration Camera frame camera_frame_id: the frame id in the camera node's CAMERA SETTINGS Camera calibration Start pose x, y, yaw of base_link on the map Initial pose

docs.title: Change Settings
docs.text:
After the upload, the settings in localizer.yaml, navigator.yaml, extrinsics.yaml and initial_pose.yaml can be changed without a new bundle:

  • Station page: select the Localizer or the Navigator node. The inspector's NAVIGATION SETTINGS section groups the keys your files contain as Localizer, Navigator, Camera calibration and Initial pose.
  • CLI: sodero navigation get --node sodero.navigator, edit the returned config, then sodero navigation apply with its SHA-256 (see sodero CLI).

Stop the Localizer, the Navigator and Visual odometry before you save; the new values apply when the nodes start again. The map files, meta.yaml and map.file change only with a new bundle. Every key is described in Map Bundle Format.

docs.title: 4. Start and Set the Initial Pose
docs.text:
1. Start the nodes in this order: the gateway and Strider, the camera gateway (and Visual odometry), the Localizer, the Navigator.
  2. Open Strider's Navigation page (the Strider link on the Navigator's card). Localization Status shows Healthy once the camera view matches the map.
  3. If the status stays Initializing or Lost, or the robot appears at the wrong place, click Set Initial Pose, press on the map where the robot stands and drag in the direction it faces (Strider › Set the Initial Pose).

The Localizer starts from the bundle's initial pose when it has no confirmed pose on this map. Once it has localized, it restarts from its last confirmed pose on the same map_id. A pose set with Set Initial Pose, or with the localization.set_initial_pose tool, replaces both. Give a changed map a new map_id so that an old pose is not reused.

Before you drive a real robot on a new map, check in simulation that the status reaches Healthy and that the robot reaches a nearby goal.

docs.title: 5. Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom or message Cause and fix … the file name must end with .tar.gz or .tgz or .tar or .zip A .nav file name on the Station page. Rename the file to site.nav.tgz. the localizer is running — stop it before replacing its bundle Stop the Localizer, then upload again. Read the current navigation SHA-256 before applying a map. The SHA-256 is out of date. Run sodero navigation get again. The status stays Initializing The camera height in the extrinsics is not measured from the floor, camera_frame_id differs from the camera's frame id, or the initial pose is far off. Fix the value or set the initial pose. The Localizer log shows camera_frame_id is required or no_extrinsics_edge extrinsics.yaml has no camera_frame_id, or no edge connects the camera's frame id to base_link. Other messages of the upload See Map Bundle Format › Validation Errors.

docs.title: Map Bundle Format
docs.text:
This page specifies the map bundle (.nav) completely: its layout, every file, every accepted key with its type, range and default, and the messages of the bundle check. It is a reference for people who build bundles. To load a finished bundle, see Load and Configure a Map; to make a bundle for your own site, see Create a Map from Your Site.

The frames map, odom, base_link and the camera's optical frame are explained in Create a Map from Your Site › Coordinate Frames.

docs.title: Bundle Layout
docs.text:
site.nav/              optional top folder, any name
├── meta.yaml          map ID and a description of the grid
├── localizer.yaml     Localizer settings, including the point-cloud file
├── navigator.yaml     Navigator settings: robot size, speeds, tolerances
├── extrinsics.yaml    camera mounting on the robot
├── initial_pose.yaml  starting pose of the robot on the map
└── map/
    ├── MAP_ID.ply     3D point cloud of the site
    ├── MAP_ID.pgm     2D occupancy grid image
    └── MAP_ID.yaml    grid resolution, origin and thresholds
File Read by meta.yaml Localizer and Navigator (the map ID) localizer.yaml, initial_pose.yaml, map/MAP_ID.ply Localizer navigator.yaml Navigator extrinsics.yaml Localizer and Visual odometry map/MAP_ID.pgm, map/MAP_ID.yaml Navigator and the map views
  • All eight files are required, and no other file is accepted. MAP_ID is the map_id of meta.yaml: the Localizer and the Navigator open the grid files by this name.
  • Archive: a gzip-compressed tar. The files sit at its root or in one top folder, which is dropped on upload. The file name does not change the format: site.nav and site.nav.tgz can be the same file.
  • Limits: the archive and its unpacked contents at most 64 MiB each, each YAML file at most 1 MiB, at most 128 archive entries including folders.
  • Names: at most 160 characters of letters, digits, _, -, . and /; no hidden names (starting with .) and no links. Map files sit directly in map/ and end in .ply, .pgm or .yaml (.yml is refused).
  • YAML: plain mappings with unique keys; unknown keys are refused. Quote dates and times, and write exponents with a decimal point: 1.0e-6 is a number, 1e-6 is read as text.

docs.title: meta.yaml
docs.text:
Key Type Unit Meaning Example schema_version integer — Always 1 1 map_id text — Map name: letters, digits, _, ., -, starting with a letter, at most 64 characters warehouse frame_id text — Map frame (default map) map created, z_slice text, [min, max] —, m Optional: creation time (quoted) and the height band used for the grid [0.05, 0.65] source mapping — Optional provenance: ply (a file name, not a path), ply_sha256, points, bbox_min, bbox_max ply: warehouse.ply grid.image, grid.yaml text — map/MAP_ID.pgm and map/MAP_ID.yaml map/warehouse.pgm grid.width, grid.height integer cells Exactly the size of the PGM 500, 620 grid.resolution number m/cell Exactly the resolution of the grid YAML 0.05 grid.origin [x, y, yaw] m, m, rad Exactly the origin of the grid YAML [-12.5, -12.5, 0.0] tool, solid_footprints, grid.min_points, grid.padding, grid.mark_unknown, grid.points_in_slice, grid.occupied_cells, grid.unknown_cells any — Optional, informational 
schema_version: 1
map_id: warehouse
created: '2026-01-15T09:00:00Z'
z_slice: [0.05, 0.65]
grid:
  image: map/warehouse.pgm
  yaml: map/warehouse.yaml
  resolution: 0.05
  width: 500
  height: 620
  origin: [-12.5, -12.5, 0.0]

docs.title: Occupancy Grid: map/MAP_ID.yaml and map/MAP_ID.pgm
docs.text:
The grid uses the standard occupancy-grid map format: a gray image and a YAML file with exactly these six keys (a key such as mode is refused).

Key Type Unit Meaning Example image text — File name of the PGM, without a folder warehouse.pgm resolution number m/cell Cell size, 0.001 to 100 0.05 origin [x, y, yaw] m, m, rad Lower-left corner of the image in map; keep yaw at 0.0 [-12.5, -12.5, 0.0] negate 0 or 1 — 1 inverts the gray values 0 occupied_thresh, free_thresh number 0 to 1 Occupancy above the first is an obstacle, below the second is free; free_thresh must be lower 0.65, 0.196 
image: warehouse.pgm
resolution: 0.05
origin: [-12.5, -12.5, 0.0]
negate: 0
occupied_thresh: 0.65
free_thresh: 0.196
  • Image: binary P5 or ASCII P2 PGM, maximum value 255, at most 16 million pixels. After the header, a P5 file holds exactly width × height bytes.
  • Values: the occupancy of a pixel is (255 − value) / 255 with negate: 0. With the thresholds above, write 0 for obstacles, 254 for free floor and 205 for unknown space.
  • Rows: row 0 is the top of the map, the largest y. The pixel in column c and row r of an image height rows tall is the cell centered at x = origin_x + (c + 0.5) × resolution, y = origin_y + (height − r − 0.5) × resolution. The warehouse grid, 500 × 620 cells of 0.05 m, covers x from −12.5 m to 12.5 m and y from −12.5 m to 18.5 m.

docs.title: Point Cloud: map/MAP_ID.ply
docs.text:
• Format: format binary_little_endian 1.0 (recommended) or format ascii 1.0, with an ASCII header in LF line endings that ends in end_header.
  • Contents: one element vertex with 1 to 2,000,000 points. The properties are x, y, z (required), nx, ny, nz and red, green, blue (optional), each of type float, double or uchar (also written float32, float64, uint8). comment lines are allowed; faces, other elements or properties (alpha, intensity, scalar fields) and lines such as obj_info are refused. The warehouse header has element vertex 1405083, then property float x, y, z, nx, ny, nz and property uchar red, green, blue.
  • Values: meters in the map frame, finite and at most 1,000,000 in magnitude. Normals, when present, must not be zero. Colors are optional (uchar 0 to 255 or float 0 to 1); without them the Localizer matches geometry only.
  • Size: binary float coordinates with normals and colors take 27 bytes per point, so 2 million points use about 54 MB of the 64 MiB limit. Use float, not double.

docs.title: extrinsics.yaml
docs.text:
Key Type Unit Meaning Example camera_frame_id text — The camera's optical frame: the frame_id in the camera node's CAMERA SETTINGS, at most 15 characters. Required by the Localizer. cam0_optical edges list — 1 to 32 fixed transforms; a frame is the child of one edge at most parent, child text — Frame names base_link, cam0_optical xyz [x, y, z] m Position of the child in the parent frame [0.22, 0.0, 0.468] quat [x, y, z, w] — Orientation of the child in the parent frame; the squares sum to 1 within 0.01 [-0.5, 0.5, -0.5, 0.5] 
camera_frame_id: cam0_optical
edges:
  - parent: base_link
    child: cam0_optical
    xyz: [0.22, 0.0, 0.468]       # 0.22 m ahead of base_link, 0.468 m above the floor
    quat: [-0.5, 0.5, -0.5, 0.5]  # level, looking forward

Rotations are written only as quat in the order [x, y, z, w]; an edge with rpy is refused. Edges may form a chain, for example base_link → mast → cam0_optical, but no loop, and they must connect the camera frame to base_link. For a camera that looks forward, tilted down by θ, quat = [-a, a, -b, b] with a = (cos(θ/2) + sin(θ/2)) / 2 and b = (cos(θ/2) − sin(θ/2)) / 2:

Tilt θ 0° (level) 10° 20° 30° quat [-0.5, 0.5, -0.5, 0.5] [-0.5417, 0.5417, -0.4545, 0.4545] [-0.5792, 0.5792, -0.4056, 0.4056] [-0.6124, 0.6124, -0.3536, 0.3536]

docs.title: initial_pose.yaml
docs.text:
Key Type Unit Meaning Example x, y number m Position of base_link (not the camera) in map -1.5984, 2.3881 yaw number rad, −π to π Heading; 0 faces the +x axis of the map 0.0 
x: -1.5984
y: 2.3881
yaw: 0.0

The Localizer starts from this pose when it has no confirmed pose on this map. Once it has localized, it restarts from its last confirmed pose on the same map_id. A pose set with Set Initial Pose on Strider's Navigation page, or with the localization.set_initial_pose tool, replaces both. Give a changed map a new map_id so that an old pose is not reused.

docs.title: localizer.yaml
docs.text:
Only map.file is required; a key you leave out keeps its default. An excerpt of the warehouse file:

map:
  file: map/warehouse.ply
  voxel_size: 0.05
icp:
  device: CPU:0
  lambda: 1.0
  max_correspondence_dist: 0.12
  max_iterations: 20
sensor: {depth_min: 0.3, depth_max: 10.0}
status: {degrade_after_s: 5.0, lost_after_s: 60.0, accept_streak: 1}
publish:
  obstacles: {z_min: 0.08, z_max: 0.65}

docs.title: Map and Frames
docs.text: Key Default Meaning map.file required The point cloud, map/MAP_ID.ply. It changes only with a new bundle. map.voxel_size 0.05 m The cell size that the map and the camera points are reduced to frames.map, frames.odom, frames.base map, odom, base_link Frame names; keep the defaults, which the Navigator also uses

docs.title: Matching
docs.text:
Key Default Meaning icp.planar true Estimate x, y and yaw only (wheeled robots); false also estimates height, roll and pitch (walking robots) icp.device CPU:0 CPU:0, or CUDA:0 for a GPU icp.rate_hz 10 Hz Localization rate icp.max_iterations 50 Iterations per camera frame icp.lambda 0.968 Weight of geometry against color, 0 to 1; 1.0 matches geometry only icp.max_correspondence_dist 0.1 m Match distance while tracking icp.init_max_correspondence_dist 0.3 m Match distance while initializing or relocalizing icp.min_fitness 0.3 A pose is accepted when at least this share of camera points matches the map… icp.max_rmse 0.05 m …within this fit error icp.max_jump_m, icp.max_jump_rad 1.0 m, 0.5 rad Largest accepted correction against the odometry prediction icp.deg_ratio, icp.deg_min_info, icp.deg_threshold 0.05, 5.0, 0 Handling of directions the view cannot observe, such as along a corridor

Advanced matching. Keep these at their defaults: icp.max_solve_points 0, icp.robust_delta 0, icp.relative_fitness 1.0e-6, icp.relative_rmse 1.0e-6, icp.min_structural_fitness 0, icp.rmse_growth_factor 1.05, icp.sigma_depth 0.01, icp.cov_inflation 4.0, icp.recovery_radius_m 0.4, icp.recovery_yaw_rad 0.5.

docs.title: Camera Points
docs.text: Key Default Meaning sensor.depth_min, sensor.depth_max 0.2 m, 6.0 m Depth range of the camera points used

docs.title: Localization Status
docs.text: Key Default Meaning status.accept_streak, status.init_min_fitness 3, 0.7 Accepted fits in a row, each with at least this fitness, needed to become Healthy (localized) status.degrade_after_s, status.lost_after_s 2.0 s, 10.0 s Time without an accepted fit before Degraded (degraded) and before Lost (lost) status.degrade_fitness 0.5 Fitness below which the state degrades status.clock_skew_ms 200 ms Largest camera-to-odometry lag status.odometry_stale_s 3.0 s Odometry silence before the input reconnects

docs.title: Recovery After Lost
docs.text: Key Default Meaning recovery.auto_reseed true After Lost, retry automatically around the last confirmed pose recovery.lost_wait_s, recovery.attempts, recovery.attempt_timeout_s, recovery.spacing_s 3.0 s, 5, 5.0 s, 1.0 s Schedule of the retries recovery.radius_step_m, recovery.max_radius_m, recovery.yaw_jitter_rad 0.3 m, 1.0 m, 0.17 rad Search area of the retries

docs.title: Outputs and Live Obstacles
docs.text: Key Default Meaning publish.pose_hz, publish.status_hz, publish.obstacles_hz 20, 1, 10 Hz Output rates publish.obstacles.z_min, publish.obstacles.z_max 0.10 m, 0.30 m Height band above the floor whose camera points mark live obstacles for the Navigator publish.obstacles.ground_relative false true measures the band from the floor seen in each image publish.obstacles.size_cells, publish.obstacles.resolution 48, 0.05 m Live obstacle grid around the robot, at most 48 × 48 cells publish.obstacles.decay_s 2.0 s How long a mark lasts

docs.title: Odometry Input and Global Search
docs.text: Key Default Meaning odometry.frame_policy match match uses only odometry from odom to base_link; any accepts a single source under any frame names odometry.recovery auto Keep auto odometry.source empty Empty follows the node connected to the Localizer's odometry port global_search.* see meaning Grid of the localization.global_search_* tools: xy_step_m 1.0, yaw_step_deg 15, coarse_radius_m 1.2, sample_radius_m 6.0, timeout_s 120, max_candidates 100000, shortlist 32, ambiguity_margin 0.08

docs.title: navigator.yaml
docs.text:
The sections are bt_navigator, planner_server, controller_server, local_costmap, global_costmap, behavior_server, velocity_smoother and navigator; section and key names follow Nav2 conventions. An excerpt of the warehouse file:

controller_server:
  general_goal_checker: {xy_goal_tolerance: 0.1, yaw_goal_tolerance: 0.1}
  FollowPath: {desired_linear_vel: 0.3, max_angular_vel: 0.5}
local_costmap:
  global_frame: odom
  rolling_window: true
  width: 4
  height: 4
  robot_radius: 0.34
  inflation_layer: {inflation_radius: 0.6}
global_costmap: {global_frame: map, robot_radius: 0.34}
velocity_smoother:
  max_velocity: [0.3, 0.0, 0.5]
  min_velocity: [-0.2, 0.0, -0.5]
navigator: {drive: diff}
  • Write the complete file. Start from the navigator.yaml of a working bundle, such as the warehouse example of Navigate in Simulation, and change values only. A key you leave out falls back to a built-in value that may not suit your robot; without robot_radius the Navigator does not start.
  • Text values are fixed: frame names, plugin entries and plugin lists keep their values. The one choice is navigator.drive: diff or holonomic.
  • Numbers are 0 to 1,000,000, except the entries of min_velocity and max_decel, which may be negative. Velocity lists have three entries: [x m/s, y m/s, yaw rad/s].
  • Robot size is a circle, robot_radius; a polygon footprint is refused.

The Template column lists the values of the reference navigator configuration, which defines the accepted keys. They are a starting point for your own values, not the built-in values used for a key you leave out.

docs.title: Robot Size and Costmaps
docs.text: Key Template Meaning local_costmap.robot_radius, global_costmap.robot_radius 0.42 m Radius around base_link that covers the robot; required, the same value in both *.inflation_layer.inflation_radius, *.inflation_layer.cost_scaling_factor 0.75 m, 3.0 Distance from obstacles within which paths cost more, and how fast that cost falls off local_costmap.width, local_costmap.height, local_costmap.resolution 6 m, 6 m, 0.05 m Size and cell size of the local window around the robot; the global costmap follows the grid's resolution *.obstacle_layer.enabled, *.obstacle_layer.decay_s true; 2.0 s local, 10.0 s global Add the Localizer's live obstacles, and how long they are kept

docs.title: Planning
docs.text: Key Template Meaning planner_server.GridBased.tolerance 0.5 m How far from a blocked goal a path may end planner_server.GridBased.allow_unknown true Plan through unknown cells planner_server.GridBased.use_astar false A* instead of Dijkstra

docs.title: Path Following
docs.text: Key Template Meaning controller_server.controller_frequency 20.0 Hz Control rate controller_server.FollowPath.desired_linear_vel, controller_server.FollowPath.max_angular_vel 1.2 m/s, 0.825 rad/s Cruise speed and turn rate limit controller_server.FollowPath.lookahead_dist, min_lookahead_dist, max_lookahead_dist 1.5, 0.6, 1.8 m Look-ahead distance on the path controller_server.FollowPath.use_rotate_to_heading, rotate_to_heading_min_angle true, 0.785 rad Turn in place toward the path when the heading error exceeds this angle controller_server.FollowPath.allow_reversing false Drive backwards along the path controller_server.FollowPath.use_holonomic_lateral, max_lateral_vel false, 0.2 m/s Move sideways (with navigator.drive: holonomic)

docs.title: Goals and Progress

docs.title: Localization and Navigation
docs.text: Stellar Station includes a complete navigation stack for mobile robots: it knows where the robot is on a map (localization) and drives it to goals around obstacles (navigation). Both run on Stellar X as built-in nodes and work with the base's Strider node: the localizer reads its odometry, and the navigator drives the base through it.

docs.title: 1. How It Works
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    CAM["Camera gateway<br>RGB-D"] -- camera --> LOC["Localizer<br>sodero.localizer"]
    STR["Strider<br>sodero.mlc.NAME"] -- odometry --> LOC
    LOC -- "localization · map" --> NAV["Navigator<br>sodero.navigator"]
    NAV -- mobile_base --> STR
    MAP[(".nav map bundle")] -.-> LOC
    MAP -.-> NAV
    STR -- servo_link --> GW["Actuator gateway"]
Node Role Camera gateway Delivers depth and color images from the robot's RGB-D camera Strider Drives the base and reports odometry: how far the wheels have moved the robot Localizer Matches the camera's 3D view against the map's point cloud and corrects the odometry, so the robot knows its pose on the map Navigator Plans a path on the map's occupancy grid and drives the base along it, avoiding obstacles, until the goal is reached Visual odometry (optional) Estimates odometry from the camera, for robots without wheel odometry such as walking robots Map bundle (.nav) One file with the map (point cloud and occupancy grid) and the localizer and navigator settings for one site (Load and Configure a Map)

By default the localizer works in the plane: it estimates x, y and heading on the map. There is one localizer and one navigator per Station, so one robot per Station navigates.

docs.title: 2. Coordinate Frames
docs.text:
Frame Meaning map The fixed frame of the map odom The odometry frame; drifts slowly as the wheels slip base_link The robot, on the floor below its center Camera optical frame The camera (for example cam0_optical): x right, y down, z forward

The localizer publishes the correction map → odom; Strider publishes odom → base_link; the map bundle's extrinsics give base_link → camera.

Because base_link is on the floor, the camera's mounting height in the extrinsics is its height above the floor, not above the robot's body frame. A wrong height makes the camera's view sink into or float above the map, and localization fails.

docs.title: 3. Set Up Navigation
docs.text:
Step Where 1. Drive the base with Strider Quick Start 2. Add a camera gateway and check its image Sensors and Cameras 3. Prepare the map bundle of the site Create a Map from Your Site, or use a finished bundle 4. Add the Localizer and the Navigator, upload the map once to the Localizer, connect the ports Load and Configure a Map, Navigate in Simulation 5. Set the initial pose and send goals Strider › Navigation Page

The connections:

From (requires) To (provides) Localizer camera Camera gateway camera Localizer odometry Strider odometry (or Visual odometry odometry) Navigator localization Localizer localization Navigator map Localizer map Navigator mobile_base Strider mobile_base

Start the nodes in this order: gateway, Strider, camera gateway, localizer, navigator. The localizer needs a running camera and an uploaded map; the navigator needs the map bundle's navigator settings.

docs.title: 4. Localization States
docs.text:
State Meaning What to do Uninitialized No pose yet Set the initial pose Initializing Searching around the initial pose Wait; keep the robot still Healthy (localized) The camera view matches the map Navigate Degraded Few recent matches (for example a featureless area or many people around) Goals are still accepted; check the camera view Lost No match for a long time; the navigator stops Set the initial pose again, or use Global localization Relocalizing A new initial pose is being checked Wait

Global localization on Strider's Navigation page searches the whole map for the robot's pose. Stop the robot before you start it, review the best candidate, and apply it.

docs.title: 5. Settings
docs.text:
The localizer and the navigator share their settings with the map bundle. Edit them in the inspector of either node under NAVIGATION SETTINGS (or with Settings on the node card), while the localizer, the navigator and visual odometry are stopped. The most useful ones:

Group Setting Meaning Navigator FollowPath.desired_linear_vel Cruise speed (m/s) max_angular_vel, rotate_to_heading_angular_vel Turning speeds (rad/s) rotate_to_heading_min_angle Above this heading error (rad), the robot turns in place before it drives. Use a small value for skid-steer bases. xy_goal_tolerance, yaw_goal_tolerance How close counts as reached (m, rad) robot_radius, inflation_radius Robot size and the clearance kept from obstacles (m) Localizer icp.max_jump_m, icp.max_jump_rad Largest correction accepted per update sensor.depth_min, sensor.depth_max Depth range of the camera used for matching (m) Initial pose x, y, yaw The pose used when no other pose is known

Uploading a map bundle again replaces these settings with the bundle's. The full list is in Map Bundle Format; from the SSH workspace use sodero navigation get and sodero navigation apply (sodero CLI).
