docs.title: 3D Model Creation
docs.text:
This tutorial assembles the 3D model of a robot arm for display in Stellar Designer, Motion Studio and the Station. It is optional. The model is for visualization only: the kinematics come from the DH parameters of the .sdd document, not from the model, and every robot runs without one. You can skip this page and add a model later.

The example is a 6-axis manipulator. Download its parts and unzip them:

  • example_manipulator_parts.zip
The example manipulator

For your own robot you need one 3D model file per link, exported from your CAD design, and the robot's DH parameters.

The steps use Blender, which reads most common 3D formats. Any other 3D tool works as long as it produces the same object names, hierarchy and file format.

docs.title: Clear the Scene
docs.text: Open Blender and delete the default Camera, Cube and Light.

docs.title: Naming Conventions
docs.text:
Part Name Base joint J0 Base link link0 Joints J1 to Jn Links link1 to linkn

n is the number of joints, 6 in this example.

docs.title: Create the Joints
docs.text: Click Add › Empty › Plain Axes to add an axis object. Add seven of them and rename them J0 to J6. Stellar Designer finds the joints by these names, so each name must be J followed by its number.

docs.title: Import the Links
docs.text:
Click File › Import › Wavefront (.obj), open the folder of the unzipped parts and import all seven parts with the import settings shown above. The scene then looks like the last picture.

Select link0 and set Rotation X to 0: the part stands upright. Repeat this for the other parts.

docs.title: Attach Each Link to Its Joint
docs.text: Select link0 and Shift-drag it onto J0, so that link0 sits under J0. Repeat this for the other links.

docs.title: 2. Build the Hierarchy
docs.text:
The robot is a serial chain: each joint is a child of the previous joint, and each link is a child of its joint.

World
└── J0
    ├── link0
    └── J1
        ├── link1
        └── J2
            ├── link2
            └── J3
                ├── link3
                └── J4
                    ├── link4
                    └── J5
                        ├── link5
                        └── J6
                            └── link6

Select J1 and Shift-drag it onto J0: J1 and link1 are now under J0. Repeat this for the other joints.

Item Description World The scene of the 3D tool J0 to Jn Joint nodes link0 to linkn Link models

Each joint Jn must be a child of the previous joint, and each link linkn a child of its joint Jn. With a different hierarchy the links do not move with their joints.

docs.title: 3. Match the DH Parameters
docs.text: The joint frames in Blender must match the DH parameters of the robot in Stellar Designer.

docs.title: DH Convention
docs.text:
Stellar Designer applies the four DH parameters of a joint in this fixed order:

  1. Rotation about Z by θ (theta)
  2. Translation along Z by d
  3. Translation along X by a
  4. Rotation about X by α (alpha)

docs.title: Place the Joints
docs.text:
J2 placed 0.205 m above J1

Joint J1 of the example has θ = 0, d = 205 mm, a = 0 and α = 0 in Stellar Designer, so the frame of J2 sits 205 mm above J1 along Z.

  1. Select J2 and set Location Z to 0.205. link2 and everything under J2 moves up.
  2. Set Location Z of J3 to 0.27 and of J5 to 0.23. The model then looks like the last picture below.

For your own robot, the parts may not line up with the joint axes of the DH parameters. In that case, move the mesh itself in your CAD program. In the assembled pose, the base is at (0, 0, 0) and every joint is at 0.

docs.title: Joint Axes
docs.text:
• Set the rotation axis of each joint Jn according to its DH parameters.
  • Rotate in the joint's local axes, not in the world axes.

docs.title: 4. Export the Model
docs.text:
1. Choose File › Export › glTF 2.0 (.glb/.gltf).

  2. In the export window, set Format to glTF Binary (.glb) and, under Transform, clear +Y Up.

Clear +Y Up. Otherwise Blender converts the model to a Y-up coordinate system, and it appears rotated in Stellar Designer.

The finished files of this example: .blend and .glb.

docs.title: 5. Load the Model in Stellar Designer
docs.text:
Open the robot's document in Stellar Designer, click Display in the 3D view and choose Load.glb (Stellar Designer). Switch Representation to 3D Model: each link moves with its joint when you jog the joints in Robot Structure. Motion Studio and the Station then show the robot with this model.

Stellar Designer uses only the .glb file.

docs.title: Articulated Robot (.sdda)
docs.text: This tutorial builds the document of a robot whose joints are driven one by one, using a four-legged robot with twelve joints as the example. The document belongs to an Articulation node (sodero.amc.NAME). Unlike a manipulator or mobile base document, it describes no kinematics: only the joints, their limits and how the gateway's actuators drive them. How the controller uses the document is described in Articulation.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
1. On the Station, add a Controller › Articulation node, for example quadruped, and an Actuator gateway for its motors (Nodes and Connections).
  2. Connect the Articulation node's servo_link to the gateway.
  3. Select the Articulation node and click Edit Stellar Designer.

A new Articulation node starts with one joint, joint_1. There are no templates; you add the joints of your robot one by one.

docs.title: Step 1: Joint Configuration
docs.text:
Joint configuration of a four-legged robot with twelve joints

Step 01 Joint configuration ① shows the controller settings on the left and the joints on the right.

Controller:

Field Meaning Controller subsystem The ID of the node. The Station fills it in. Actuator gateway The gateway connected to the node's servo_link. The Station fills it in. Drive mode ② Position targets: the controller bounds the joint targets, and the drive (or the simulated joint) follows them with its own position control. Set a matching effort limit in the drive or the simulator.Bounded PD torque: the controller computes a torque from each joint's Kp and Kd and clamps it to the joint's torque limit.

Joints: Add joint ③ adds a joint at the end of the list, up to 64 joints. Open a joint ④ to edit it:

Field Meaning Name A unique name of letters, digits and underscores Min, Max (rad) Range of motion. Targets outside it are refused. Speed (rad/s) Velocity limit, also the reference for the jog speed in Articulation Torque (N·m) Torque limit Offset (rad) Joint position at actuator position zero Kp, Kd Stiffness and damping, shown in Bounded PD torque mode

Move up moves a joint one place up and Remove deletes it.

Each leg of the example robot (fl, fr, rl, rr) has a hip, a thigh and a calf joint, named for example fl_hip. The list runs leg by leg: fl_hip, fl_thigh, fl_calf, then the joints of fr, rl and rr. The example uses these values; enter those of your own robot:

Hip Thigh Calf Min (rad) −0.8 −1.0 −2.7 Max (rad) 0.8 3.0 −0.9 Speed (rad/s) 20 20 20 Torque (N·m) 25 25 35

Joint order matters. Commands and feedback follow the order of the list. A program that sends joint targets must use the same order: Legged locomotion, for example, compares the joint names and their order with its walking policy and does not start if they differ (The controller joint order does not match the policy manifest.).

Save configuration ⑤ saves the document to the node; the button shows Saved when there is nothing left to save. Stellar Designer also saves when you return to the Station.

docs.title: Step 2: Actuator Mapping
docs.text:
Twelve actuators, each driving one joint

The canvas ① shows the gateway's actuators (top) and the joints (bottom); the right panel ② lists the INFLUENCE FACTOR of each connection. Every joint you add starts connected to the actuator with the same number, with factor 1.

Change the mapping as for a manipulator (Manipulator › Actuator Mapping): drag from an actuator's connector to a joint's connector, set the influence factor, and use a negative factor to reverse a direction. Several connections describe coupled joints. The mapping uses as many actuators as there are joints, and it must be invertible: every set of joint targets must correspond to exactly one set of actuator commands.

Actuator n here is actuator n of the gateway. The gateway must provide at least as many actuators as the document has joints.

docs.title: Save a Copy
docs.text: To save the document to your computer, click the Stellar mark at the top left and choose Definition › Download .sdda. You can import the file into another Articulation node with Import .sdda (Design Documents).

docs.title: Try the Robot
docs.text:
Real hardware moves. Support a legged robot so that its feet are off the ground, keep the area clear and keep the emergency stop within reach.

Start the gateway, then the Articulation node, and click Articulation in the node's CONTROL section (Articulation). Switch the servo on and jog each joint at a low speed. Check that:

  • each joint moves in the expected direction,
  • each joint stops at its limits,
  • the joint monitor shows the expected angles in a known pose. Correct a joint's zero with Offset, or with Set origin in Articulation.

This guide ends with this manual joint test. A program that sends joint targets, such as Legged locomotion with a walking policy, needs its own preparation, which this documentation does not cover: its joint names and order must match the document (Step 1), and it must be tested with the robot supported off the ground.

docs.title: Stellar Designer
docs.text:
Stellar Designer creates and edits the design documents of gateways and controllers: the robot's structure, its limits and safety settings, and how the gateway's actuators drive its joints or wheels. Each actuator gateway and controller node on the Station holds one document:

Document Describes Node Page .gw The actuators and the hardware that drives them (EtherCAT drives or Isaac Sim) Actuator gateway Gateway Designer (.gw) .sdd Manipulator (serial arm) Motion Studio Manipulator (.sdd) .sddm Wheeled mobile base Strider Mobile Robot (.sddm) .sdda Articulated robot driven joint by joint (legged robots, humanoids) Articulation Articulated Robot (.sdda)

A 3D model (.glb) for display is optional (3D Model Creation). This page covers the controller documents; gateway documents are edited in the Gateway Designer, the part of Stellar Designer for .gw files.

docs.title: 1. Open Stellar Designer
docs.text:
1. On the Station, select a controller node (Motion Studio, Strider or Articulation).
  2. Click Edit Stellar Designer in the node's DEFINITION section.

Stellar Designer opens in a new tab with the node's document. Changes are saved back to the node automatically; in an Articulation document, click Save configuration. Stop the node before you edit its document; the new document takes effect the next time the node starts.

If a Motion Studio or Strider node has no document yet, Stellar Designer opens Create robot definition: choose a template of the robot type, or Blank robot for a manipulator, and click Create. An Articulation node starts with a document of one joint.

Robot type Templates Manipulator 2-axis two-bar arm, 4-axis SCARA, 4-axis cylindrical SCARA, 7-axis humanoid arm, Blank robot Mobile Differential drive 2WD, MiR250 differential, Skid steer 4WD, Mecanum 4WD, Swerve 4WD, Ackermann

You can also import a document you already have with Import in the node's DEFINITION section (Design Documents).

docs.title: 2. Screen Layout
docs.text: Stellar Designer with a 6-axis arm Area Description Breadcrumb Where the document belongs: device / Station / node / file. The arrow returns to the Station. Steps 01 Robot Structure (or Chassis Structure for mobile robots), 02 Robot System Parameters, 03 Actuator Mapping, 04 Verification. An Articulation document has two steps: 01 Joint configuration and 02 Actuator Mapping. Click a step to open it; you can go back and forth. Left panel The joints (or wheels) of the robot, with their parameters 3D view The robot as you define it. Drag to rotate, right-drag to pan, scroll to zoom. Fit view frames the robot; Focus selection frames the selected part. Right panel Details of the selection, such as constraints, or the parameters of the current step Units mm / g / deg or m / kg / radian. Display only; documents store SI units.

docs.title: Display Menu
docs.text:
The Display menu

Display in the 3D view switches between Skeleton (joint frames and links as lines) and 3D Model, and shows or hides Joint frames, Grid and Axis gizmo. Load.glb attaches the robot's 3D model, a GLB file, to the document; Motion Studio and the Station then show the robot with it (3D Model Creation).

docs.title: 3. Workflow
docs.text:
1. Structure. Define the joints (manipulator) or the chassis and wheels (mobile robot).
  2. System parameters. Enter the robot-wide values: payload, gravity, speed limits, goal tolerances, safety margins.
  3. Actuator mapping. Connect the gateway's actuators to the joints or wheels, with their transmission factors.
  4. Verification. Click Verify. When all checks pass, the document is ready; Export saves a copy to your computer.

An Articulation document has only the joints with their limits and the actuator mapping (Articulated Robot).

Then start the node on the Station and try the robot, in simulation first.

docs.title: Manipulator (.sdd)
docs.text: This guide walks through the four steps of a manipulator document. The document belongs to a Motion Studio node (sodero.mmc.NAME), which drives the arm through an actuator gateway. The pictures show a 6-axis arm; there is no downloadable example arm, so you enter the data of your own arm.

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
1. On the Station, add a Controller › Motion Studio node, for example arm, and an Actuator gateway for its motors (Nodes and Connections).
  2. Select the Motion Studio node and click Edit Stellar Designer. For a new node, choose a template or Blank robot in Create robot definition.

You need the arm's kinematics as DH parameters (from its datasheet or CAD), its joint limits, and, for accurate gravity compensation and collision detection, the mass properties of its links.

docs.title: Step 1: Robot Structure
docs.text:
Robot Structure: joints, DH parameters and constraints

Step 01 Robot Structure ① shows the Joint Section: the joints from the base to the tool flange.

  1. Click Add joint ⑥ to add a joint at the end of the chain. The trash icon removes a joint.
  2. Open a joint ② and choose its Joint Type ③: rotation or translation about the joint's X, Y or Z axis.
  3. Enter its DH PARAMETERS ④: DH (Theta), DH (D), DH (A) and DH (Alpha). The 3D view updates as you type.
  4. Under ADVANCED SETTINGS:
    • Dynamics: the mass, center of mass and inertia of the link that moves with this joint.
    • Constraints ⑤: opens the joint's constraints in the right panel ⑧.
  5. Use JOG + / − to move the joint in the 3D view and check its direction. Jog Reset returns all joints to zero.

Joint constraints ⑧:

Group Fields Meaning JOINT LIMITS Lower Limit, Upper Limit Range of motion of the joint KINEMATIC LIMITS Max Speed, Max Accel, Max Jerk Limits of trajectories in joint space FRICTION PARAMETERS w1, f1, w2, f2, Max Friction Friction model used by the dynamics (velocity and torque breakpoints) COLLISION THRESHOLD Collision Threshold Residual torque above which the controller detects a collision and stops GOAL TOLERANCE Joint Goal How close a joint must be for a motion to count as finished

Display ⑦ switches the 3D view between the skeleton and the robot's 3D model (Stellar Designer).

docs.title: Step 2: Robot System Parameters
docs.text:
General Safety (Advanced)

General:

Group Fields Meaning ROBOT Arm reach, Max payload, Max allowable inertia Size and payload rating of the arm ENVIRONMENT Gravity vector Direction and size of gravity in the base frame; (0, 0, -9.81) m/s² for a floor-mounted arm. Change it for wall or ceiling mounting. MOTION Task space limit: Max speed, Max accel, Max jerk Limits of the tool in Cartesian motions GOAL TOLERANCE Position, Orientation How close the tool must be for a Cartesian motion to count as finished

Safety (Advanced):

Group Fields Meaning WARNING Revolute margin, Prismatic margin, Velocity ratio, Torque ratio Distance to a joint limit, or fraction of a speed or torque limit, at which the controller warns PROTECTIVE STOP the same fields Thresholds at which the controller stops the robot EMERGENCY STOP Comm timeout, Max overrun Emergency stop when the gateway's feedback is missing for longer than Comm timeout, or the control loop overruns for longer than Max overrun Clear grace After a protective stop is cleared, joint position limits are not checked for this time, so the robot can move back from the limit

docs.title: Step 3: Actuator Mapping
docs.text:
Six actuators, each driving one joint

The canvas shows the gateway's actuators (top) and the robot's joints (bottom).

  1. Drag from an actuator's connector to a joint's connector to connect them. A new arm starts with Actuator n connected to Joint n.
  2. In the right panel, set the INFLUENCE FACTOR of each connection: how many joint units one actuator unit moves, after the gear. Use 1 for a direct joint, a negative value to reverse the direction, and several connections for coupled joints (such as a differential wrist).
  3. The trash icon removes a connection.

The gear ratio of each motor belongs to the gateway's document, not here (Gateway Designer).

docs.title: Step 4: Verification
docs.text:
1. Click Verify. Stellar Designer checks the robot structure, the system parameters, the actuator mapping and the configuration files of the document.
  2. Open a group to see each check. Fix any errors and click Verify again.
All checks passed

Export .sdd saves a copy of the document to your computer, for backup or for other Stations.

docs.title: Try the Arm
docs.text:
1. Return to the Station, connect the Motion Studio node's servo_link to the gateway, and start the gateway and the Motion Studio node.
  2. Open Stellar Motion Studio from the node and jog each joint slowly. Check that every joint moves in the direction and by the angle you expect (Motion Studio).

Tip: Try a new document in Isaac Sim first (Virtual Simulation). Errors in DH parameters or joint directions are easy to see there and harmless.

docs.title: Mobile Robot (.sddm)
docs.text: This tutorial builds the document of a wheeled mobile base, using the Clearpath Jackal (skid steer, four wheels) of the Quick Start. The document belongs to a Strider node (sodero.mlc.NAME).

docs.title: Before You Start
docs.text:
1. On the Station, add a Controller › Strider node, for example jackal, and an Actuator gateway for its wheel motors (Nodes and Connections).
  2. Select the Strider node and click Edit Stellar Designer.
  3. In Create robot definition, choose the template that matches your drive:
Template Drive Differential drive 2WD Two driven wheels and casters MiR250 differential Differential drive of a MiR250 Skid steer 4WD Four fixed driven wheels that slide when turning Mecanum 4WD Four mecanum wheels, omnidirectional Swerve 4WD Four steered and driven wheels Ackermann Car-like steering

The template sets the drive type, which decides how body velocities become wheel commands. Then change its dimensions to those of your robot.

docs.title: Step 1: Chassis Structure
docs.text:
Chassis Structure of a skid-steer base

Step 01 Chassis Structure ① shows the body and the wheels of the base.

Body ②:

Field Meaning Template The drive type Length, Width, Height Outer dimensions of the body Base Origin Z Height of the robot's base frame above the floor (normally the wheel radius) Track Width Distance between the left and right wheels of a differential drive

Wheels ③ (Wheel-fl, Wheel-fr, Wheel-rl, Wheel-rr):

Field Meaning Role drive (driven), steer (steered), drive + steering, or caster (passive) Radius, Width Wheel size Offset X, Offset Y, Offset Z Wheel position relative to the base frame (X forward, Y left)

Constraints ④ opens the wheel's drive limits in the right panel ⑥: max_speed and max_accel of the wheel.

The constraints of the front-left wheel, with its diameter and width in the 3D view

Display ⑤ changes the 3D view; the unit menu ⑦ changes the display units.

Skid-steer wheels slide sideways when the robot turns, so the robot turns less than the wheel speeds suggest. The skid-steer kinematics use the wheels' Offset Y: turn the robot in place by a known angle and increase the left and right Offset Y until the odometry matches the real turn. The simulated Jackal of the Quick Start, for example, uses an effective Offset Y of 0.441 m.

docs.title: Step 2: Robot System Parameters
docs.text: Robot System Parameters of the Jackal Group Fields Meaning ROBOT Total mass, Max payload, Center of mass, Body inertia Mass properties of the robot ENVIRONMENT Gravity vector Normally (0, 0, -9.81) m/s² MOTION Max linear speed, Max angular speed, Max linear accel, Max angular accel Limits of the body velocity. Strider and the Navigator never exceed them.

docs.title: Step 3: Actuator Mapping
docs.text:
Four actuators driving the four wheels

Connect each actuator of the gateway to the wheel it drives (or steers), as for a manipulator (Manipulator › Actuator Mapping). The order must match the gateway: in the Jackal's gateway, actuator 1 is the front-left wheel, 2 front-right, 3 rear-left, 4 rear-right.

A mobile base uses the mapping only to know which actuator drives which wheel; leave the INFLUENCE FACTOR at 1. The wheel kinematics already account for the left and right side. If a real wheel still turns the wrong way, invert the motor's direction in its drive, for example by writing the drive's polarity parameter as a start-up SDO (EtherCAT Gateway).

docs.title: Step 4: Verification
docs.text:
Click Verify. Stellar Designer checks the chassis structure, the system parameters, the actuator mapping and the configuration files.

All checks passed: skid steer, 4 wheels, 4 actuators

Export .sddm saves a copy of the document to your computer.

docs.title: Try the Robot
docs.text:
Start the gateway and the Strider node, open Strider, choose Twist, switch the servo on and drive slowly (Strider). Check that:

  • Forward drives forward and every wheel turns the right way,
  • Turn Left turns counterclockwise (seen from above),
  • the odometry on the Status page matches the distance and angle actually driven.

docs.title: Connect to Stellar Station
docs.text: With Isaac Bridge installed and the robot prepared, point the Station's gateways at Isaac Sim and drive the robot.

docs.title: 1. Play the Scene
docs.text:
1. Open the scene in Isaac Sim and press Play.
  2. Open Window › Isaac Bridge and check that the ports are serving and your robot is bound.
① ports serving ② robots bound ③ cameras served ④ Rescan

docs.title: 2. Set the Gateways on the Station
docs.text:
Set the Station nodes to match Isaac Sim:

Isaac Sim Station node Field Robot jackal Actuator gateway (simulation) TARGET › Robot name jackal The Isaac Sim computer Actuator gateway (simulation) TARGET › Sim host: the computer's IP address Camera cam0 Camera gateway Camera name cam0, Camera host: the computer's IP address, Port 53335 Robot jackal (with an IMU) IMU gateway Robot in World jackal

The IMU gateway has no host field: it connects to the simulator address configured for your controller, which Sodero support sets (Sensors and Cameras).

The Robot name on the Station must be exactly the robot's prim name in Isaac Sim. Names are case-sensitive. If they differ, the gateway keeps waiting and the robot never moves.

Robot name and Sim host of a simulation gateway

How to create the gateways and their documents: Simulation Gateway, Sensors and Cameras.

docs.title: 3. Start and Drive
docs.text:
1. Start the gateways, then the controllers (Running Nodes).
  2. Each simulation gateway logs Simulator connected.
  3. Open the controller's UI, switch the servo on, and jog: Strider for mobile bases, Motion Studio for manipulators.
The Jackal jogged from Strider

docs.title: 4. Stop, Pause and Play
docs.text:
The gateways treat Isaac Sim like a power supply of real drives:

In Isaac Sim Result Pause The robots stay where they are. The gateways see the simulator stop and switch the servo off; switch it on again after you resume. Stop, then Play A new session: the robots start again at their authored pose, as after a power cycle. Switch the servo on again. Editing the scene while it plays Takes effect at the next Play, or click Rescan in the Isaac Bridge window Closing Isaac Sim and starting it again The gateways lose the simulator, and the controllers stop the robots. When the scene plays again, restart the robot's nodes from the toolbar: Stop all nodes, then Start all nodes (Running Nodes). Switch the servo on again.

After the simulation restarts, the robot is back at its starting pose, but the Localizer may still hold its last pose. If Strider's Navigation page shows a wrong pose, set the initial pose again.

docs.title: 5. Several Robots
docs.text:
One scene can hold several robots. Add one gateway (and controller) per robot on the Station, each with its own Robot name. All gateways use the same Isaac Sim computer and ports; the status window lists every robot it serves.

A robot can also be driven by several gateways, for example an arm and its gripper. Each gateway drives its own range of joints, set by its DOF offset (Gateway Designer).

docs.title: 6. Real-Time Performance
docs.text:
The simulation runs in real time while the computer keeps up with the render rate. The controllers follow the simulation's time, but camera-based localization runs on wall-clock time, so a simulation that runs slower than real time degrades localization.

  • Use moderate camera sizes and frame rates; each camera is rendered in addition to the viewport.
  • Close viewports and windows you do not need.
  • Do not run other heavy GPU programs (such as training) on the same computer at the same time.
  • Keep the clocks of both computers synchronized (NTP). The camera gateway accepts frames at most 20 ms ahead of and 2 s behind its own clock. If you cannot synchronize them, start Isaac Sim with RC_CAMERA_CAPTURE_TIME=0: the camera gateway then stamps each frame when it arrives.

docs.title: 7. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Cause and fix The status window does not show serving Another program (for example a second Isaac Sim) holds ports 53333–53335. Close it and press Play again. Gateway log stays at waiting for it to start Isaac Sim is not playing, Sim host is wrong, or a firewall blocks the ports (Isaac Bridge Installation) Isaac Sim console: 'sim_command' for 'X', which is no robot or tracked object of this stage The gateway's Robot name X is not the prim name of a robot in the scene The robot is listed but never bound It is not a valid PhysX articulation, or its name is used twice (Robot Setup) Camera gateway: publishes frames of camera(s) … but none of camera … The camera gateway's Camera name is not the camera's prim name Camera gateway: frames stale or with capture times that do not match The clocks of the two computers differ. Synchronize them, or start Isaac Sim with RC_CAMERA_CAPTURE_TIME=0 so that the camera gateway uses arrival times. The robot moves too fast or too slow The computer cannot keep up with the render rate. Lower camera sizes or rates, or close viewports.

The Isaac Sim console shows the bridge's messages, prefixed with the robot or camera name.

docs.title: Isaac Bridge Installation
docs.text: Isaac Bridge is the Isaac Sim extension that connects Isaac Sim to the gateways of Stellar Station. Install it once on the computer that runs Isaac Sim.

docs.title: 1. Download the Extension
docs.text:
Isaac Bridge is open source. Download release v1.0.0, the version this documentation is verified with (Compatibility), from GitHub:

git clone --branch v1.0.0 https://github.com/Sodero-labs/isaac_bridge.git

Or download the source ZIP file of release v1.0.0 from the repository's Releases page, extract it, and rename the extracted folder isaac_bridge-1.0.0 to isaac_bridge. Either way you get a folder isaac_bridge. Remember the folder that contains it, for example ~/isaac_extensions when the extension is in ~/isaac_extensions/isaac_bridge.

Updating. When you install another release, replace the folder, restart Isaac Sim and check the connection again: the status window shows the ports serving and your robots bound, and each simulation gateway logs Simulator connected.

docs.title: 2. Add the Extension to Isaac Sim
docs.text:
1. Start Isaac Sim.
  2. Open Window › Extensions.
  3. Open the Extensions window's settings (the menu icon next to the search field) and add the folder that contains isaac_bridge to Extension Search Paths.
  4. Search for isaac bridge ①.
  5. Switch the extension on ②.
  6. Tick AUTOLOAD ③, so the extension starts with Isaac Sim from now on.
① search ② enable ③ autoload

When the extension starts the first time, Isaac Sim installs the Python package pyzmq from the internet. For a computer without internet access, download the package on a computer that has internet access and the same operating system and Isaac Sim version, copy the wheels folder to the Isaac Sim computer, and install it from there. Run the commands in Isaac Sim's installation folder:

LinuxWindows 
# On the computer with internet access
./python.sh -m pip download pyzmq -d wheels
# On the Isaac Sim computer, with the copied wheels folder
./python.sh -m pip install --no-index --find-links wheels pyzmq

REM On the computer with internet access
python.bat -m pip download pyzmq -d wheels
REM On the Isaac Sim computer, with the copied wheels folder
python.bat -m pip install --no-index --find-links wheels pyzmq

You can also start Isaac Sim with the extension from a command line: isaac-sim.sh --ext-folder ~/isaac_extensions --enable isaac_bridge (isaac-sim.bat on Windows).

docs.title: 3. Open the Status Window
docs.text:
Open Window › Isaac Bridge. The window shows what the bridge serves. Before a scene plays it is mostly empty; press Play in Isaac Sim and it fills in:

The Isaac Bridge status window while a scene plays No. Line Meaning 1 Ports The command (53333), state (53334) and camera (53335) ports, and serving when the gateways can connect. The line below shows the scene's physics and render rates. 2 Robots Every robot of the scene: its name, its prim path, bound when the bridge controls it, and its number of joints (DOF) 3 Cameras Every camera served: name, resolution, frame rate and frames sent 4 Rescan Looks for robots and cameras again after you changed the scene while it plays

The ports open when the scene plays and close when it stops.

docs.title: 4. Allow the Ports in the Firewall
docs.text:
Stellar X connects to the Isaac Sim computer on TCP ports 53333, 53334 and 53335. Allow them for incoming connections from Stellar X.

Ubuntu (ufw)Windows 
sudo ufw allow from <Stellar X IP address> to any port 53333:53335 proto tcp

Open Windows Defender Firewall › Advanced settings › Inbound Rules › New Rule…, choose Port, TCP, ports 53333-53335, and allow the connection for your private network.

The bridge does not authenticate its clients: any computer that reaches these ports can command the robots of the scene. Use it on a trusted network only, and do not open the ports to the internet.

docs.title: 5. Update or Remove
docs.text:
• Update: run git pull in the isaac_bridge folder (or replace the folder with a newer release) and restart Isaac Sim.
  • Remove: switch the extension off in Window › Extensions, untick AUTOLOAD, and remove its folder from Extension Search Paths.

The extension's README describes advanced settings, such as camera sizes and rates, which cameras to publish, and the ports.

Next: Robot Setup.

docs.title: Virtual Simulation with Isaac Sim
docs.text:
The example scene of the Quick Start: a Clearpath Jackal and a Clearpath Dingo in a warehouse

NVIDIA Isaac Sim is a robotics simulator with physically based rendering and GPU physics. With the Isaac Bridge extension, Isaac Sim becomes the simulator of Stellar X: the controllers on the Station drive robots in Isaac Sim through simulation gateways, with the same commands they send to real motors.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph SX ["Stellar X · Stellar Station"]
        CTRL["Controllers<br>Motion Studio · Strider · Articulation"] --> AG["Simulation gateways<br>(actuator)"]
        IG["IMU gateways"]
        CG["Camera gateways"]
    end
    subgraph PC ["Isaac Sim computer"]
        IB["Isaac Bridge extension"] --- ST["Scene<br>robots · cameras"]
    end
    AG -- "joint commands · 53333" --> IB
    IB -- "joint states · 53334" --> AG
    IB -- "IMU · 53334" --> IG
    IB -- "RGB-D frames · 53335" --> CG
  • Gateways connect the simulator. A simulation gateway replaces the fieldbus with the network connection to Isaac Sim. The controllers, their documents and your applications are the same as for the real robot. On the real robot you also verify the actuator mapping, calibration, limits and sensor settings.
  • Simulated joints behave like servo drives. Each joint receives position, velocity or torque commands and reports its position, velocity and torque, like a drive with its motor and encoder.
  • Cameras and IMUs of the scene are served to the Station's camera and IMU gateways, so localization, navigation and walking controllers run on simulated sensors.
  • Several robots can share one scene. Each robot has a unique name, and each gateway on the Station names the robot it drives.

What you can do in simulation:

  • Check kinematics, joint directions and limits before the first power-on of a real robot.
  • Develop and test applications, navigation and mission logic without hardware.
  • Test multi-robot scenarios and sites that do not exist yet.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Item Requirement Isaac Sim 6.0, on Linux or Windows (Isaac Sim requirements and installation). Isaac Bridge 1.0.0 is verified with Isaac Sim 6.0 (Compatibility). Isaac Bridge The Sodero extension for Isaac Sim (Isaac Bridge Installation) Network Stellar X and the Isaac Sim computer on the same network; Stellar X must reach the Isaac Sim computer on TCP ports 53333–53335 Clock Both computers synchronized with a time server (NTP), when you use cameras

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
Step Page 1. Install Isaac Sim and the Isaac Bridge extension Isaac Bridge Installation 2. Prepare the robot in the scene: articulation, name, joint order, cameras Robot Setup 3. Point the Station's gateways at Isaac Sim and run Connect to Stellar Station

Tip: The Quick Start uses a prepared Jackal scene and its example files. Do step 1 first; the Quick Start then covers steps 2 and 3 for the Jackal.

docs.title: Robot Setup
docs.text: Isaac Bridge serves every robot of the open scene that follows a few rules. This page explains them and how to prepare your own robot. Scenes exported by Sodero already follow them, and so does the example scene of the Quick Start (jackal_warehouse.usd): open it to see a working example.

docs.title: 1. The Rules
docs.text:
Rule Why The robot is a PhysX articulation. Its top prim carries an Articulation Root. The bridge finds robots by their articulation root. The prim name is the robot name. It is unique in the scene and equal to the Robot name of the robot's gateway on the Station. Gateways address robots by this name. The joints, in their USD order, are the actuators. Actuator 1 of the gateway is the robot's first movable joint, actuator 2 the second, and so on. Links are under links, joints under joints. Sensors refer to links by their name under links. Z up, meters. Joint values are exchanged in radians (revolute joints) and meters (prismatic joints).

A robot prepared this way looks like this in the Stage panel:

① the robot prim jackal with the Articulation Root ② its four drive joints in actuator order 
/World/jackal              ← Articulation Root; prim name = robot name
    links/
        base_link          ← rigid body (with cameras below it)
        wheel_fl, wheel_fr, wheel_rl, wheel_rr
    joints/
        drive_fl           ← actuator 1
        drive_fr           ← actuator 2
        drive_rl           ← actuator 3
        drive_rr           ← actuator 4

docs.title: 2. Start from a Model
docs.text:
• Isaac Sim assets. Isaac Sim ships many robots from well-known manufacturers. Find them in the Isaac Sim Assets browser (Window › Browsers).
  • URDF. Import a URDF with Isaac Sim's URDF importer (File › Import). See Import URDF in the Isaac Sim documentation.
  • A 3D model. Rig the robot yourself: rigid bodies and colliders on the links, joints between them, and an articulation root. See Articulate a Basic Robot in the Isaac Sim documentation.

Then check the model against the rules above; the sections below show how to fix what differs.

docs.title: 3. Articulation Root and Name
docs.text:
1. Select the robot's top prim in the Stage panel, for example /World/jackal.
  2. Right-click it and choose Add › Physics › Articulation Root. A robot has exactly one articulation root; remove any other articulation root inside the robot.
  3. Rename the prim to the robot name. Use lowercase letters, digits and _, and start with a letter.

The robot name must be unique in the scene. If two prims share a name, only one of them is served.

Fixed-base robots (manipulators) are fixed to the world by a Fixed Joint from the world to their base link. Create it inside the robot (select the base link, Create › Physics › Joint › Fixed Joint) and leave Body 0 empty, which means the world. Mobile and walking robots have no such joint.

docs.title: 4. Joints and Drives
docs.text:
Joint order. Actuator i of the gateway is the i-th revolute or prismatic joint under the robot prim, in the order the joints are stored in the USD file. The Stage panel shows this order when it is sorted Old to New (the default). Fixed joints do not count.

Gateway Isaac Sim Actuator 1 (index 0) 1st movable joint Actuator 2 (index 1) 2nd movable joint … …

When the order of the scene differs from the order your controller document expects, change the actuator mapping in the document, or re-create the joints in the order you need.

Drives. Give every actuated joint a drive: right-click the joint and choose Add › Physics › Angular Drive (revolute) or Linear Drive (prismatic). The bridge sets the drive gains for each command mode. Set the drive's Max Force to the joint's real torque or force limit.

Limits and zero. The joint's lower and upper limits and its zero position come from the USD joint. Make the zero position match the zero of the real robot, so that the same document works for both.

Starting pose. Each time the scene plays, the robot starts where it was authored: its root at its position in the scene and every joint at its authored joint state, or at zero. Velocities start at zero.

Passive joints. Joints that are not actuators, such as caster wheels, are marked with the attribute rc:passive = true on the joint; they then do not count in the actuator order.

docs.title: 5. Physics and Mass
docs.text:
• Every link is a rigid body with a collider and a realistic mass. Wrong masses make torques, hand guiding and walking unrealistic.
  • Wheels need friction: give the floor and the wheels a physics material with realistic friction.
  • The bridge runs physics at the rate authored on the scene's PhysicsScene prim (rc:physicsHz) and renders at rc:renderHz. Without them it uses 60 Hz for both. Use at least 120 Hz physics for mobile robots and higher rates for walking robots; a lower render rate (20–30 Hz) leaves more time for physics. The render rate is lowered automatically so that each rendered frame runs a whole number of physics steps.

The current rates appear in the Isaac Bridge status window.

docs.title: 6. Cameras
docs.text:
Every Camera prim of the scene (except Isaac Sim's own viewport cameras) is served under its prim name, with color and depth images (640 × 480 at 15 frames per second by default). Cameras render only while the scene plays.

The camera cam0 under the Jackal's base_link
  1. Create a camera under the link it is mounted on (Create › Camera), for example /World/jackal/links/base_link/cam0, so it moves with the robot.
  2. Place and point it as on the real robot.
  3. Give it a unique name. The Station's camera gateway uses this name as Camera name.
  4. Note its horizontal field of view: the camera gateway needs it (Sensors and Cameras). Isaac Bridge prints each camera's field of view in the Isaac Sim console when the scene plays.

To change a camera's size or frame rate, or to publish only some cameras, follow Cameras in the extension's README.

docs.title: 7. IMU
docs.text:
Walking robots and visual odometry need an IMU. The bridge emulates an IMU on a link of the robot when the robot prim carries these attributes:

Attribute (on the robot prim) Type Meaning rc:imuLink string Name of the link under links that carries the IMU, for example base_link rc:imuOffset float3 Position of the IMU in that link's frame, in meters (default 0, 0, 0)

The Station's IMU gateway then reads it under the robot name (Sensors and Cameras).

docs.title: 8. Add Attributes with the Script Editor
docs.text:
Attributes such as rc:physicsHz, rc:imuLink or rc:passive are custom USD attributes. Add them with Window › Script Editor, then save the scene (File › Save):

import omni.usd
from pxr import Gf, Sdf

stage = omni.usd.get_context().get_stage()

# physics and render rates of the scene
scene = stage.GetPrimAtPath("/World/PhysicsScene")
scene.CreateAttribute("rc:physicsHz", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.Float).Set(120.0)
scene.CreateAttribute("rc:renderHz", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.Float).Set(30.0)

# an IMU on the base link of my_robot, 5 cm above the link origin
robot = stage.GetPrimAtPath("/World/my_robot")
robot.CreateAttribute("rc:imuLink", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.String).Set("base_link")
robot.CreateAttribute("rc:imuOffset", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.Float3).Set(Gf.Vec3f(0.0, 0.0, 0.05))

# a caster that is not an actuator
caster = stage.GetPrimAtPath("/World/my_robot/joints/caster_joint")
caster.CreateAttribute("rc:passive", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.Bool).Set(True)

Replace the prim paths with those of your scene.
